items.title: American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria: Accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Chun SG, Iyengar P, Rimner A, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: While accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy has increasingly been adopted in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy, there is a paucity of randomized prospective evidence guiding utilization. Given the marked heterogeneity in the presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, the American Radium Society (ARS) Thoracic Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) Panel evaluated the appropriateness of accelerated hypofractionation in the context of multidisciplinary management. Methods: Five clinical variants representing manifestations of locally-advanced NSCLC were developed by the 15-member multidisciplinary ARS Thoracic AUC panel. The English-language medical literature was formally reviewed from 2010-2025 and scrutinized for prospective clinical trials utilizing accelerated hypofractionation for concurrent chemotherapy ineligible patients. All case variants were evaluated with respect to use of radiation technique, radiation fractionation, and utilization of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy with Modified Delphi methodology. Consensus recommendations were reviewed and approved by the ARS Executive Committee and subject to public comment. Results: The literature review identified 228 articles, of which there were 14 prospective trials/registries including nine Phase I-II trials, four prospective registries, and one randomized Phase III trial. There was consensus that it is appropriate to utilize intensity modulated radiation therapy and proton therapy across presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, with the aim of constraining the lung V20Gy<30% and heart V40Gy<20% with accelerated hypofractionation. When utilizing 15-fraction accelerated hypofractionation for disease abutting the esophagus or brachial plexus, there was consensus that it is inappropriate to exceed doses of 45-55 Gy. With respect to PD-L1 immunotherapy, there was consensus that consolidative immunotherapy after definitive radiation therapy is appropriate, but that concurrent immunotherapy is inappropriate. There was panel consensus that it may be appropriate to utilize induction PD-L1 immunotherapy prior to radiation therapy in cases of bulky or N3 disease to test disease biology. Across variants, there was consensus that conventionally fractionated radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions remains appropriate.…

items.title: Treatment of Advanced Biliary Tract Cancer: ASCO Living Guideline, Version 2026.1.0
items.authors: Shroff RT, Kennedy EB, Alarcon Rozas AE, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This living guideline provides recommendations for liquid biopsy and treatment of patients with advanced biliary tract cancer. Methods: The American Society of Clinical Oncology convened an Expert Panel to conduct a systematic review of relevant studies and develop recommendations for liquid biopsy and systemic therapy for patients with advanced biliary tract cancer. Results: Six studies provided estimates of concordance between liquid biopsy and tissue biopsy. Nine RCTs were included in the evidence base for first-line therapy. One phase III RCT and four phase II RCTs were included in the evidence for second-line chemotherapy. Eleven single studies or reviews supported biomarker-specific second-line therapy recommendations. Recommendations: Testing with broad-based tissue DNA and RNA NGS testing to determine the presence of targetable biomarkers is recommended at the time of diagnosis at any stage. Liquid biopsy with plasma is generally recommended only when tissue biopsy is unavailable. As first-line therapy for patients with pMMR/MSS advanced BTC, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) plus chemotherapy is recommended. Options for patients with advanced BTC who are not candidates for ICIs are included in the guideline. Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an option for patients with dMMR/MSI-H advanced BTC. For patients with disease progression on first-line treatment and who have no identified biomarkers, FOLFOX with active symptom control, or active symptom control alone are recommended; options for patients who are ineligible for oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy are included in the guideline. Second-line therapy options are recommended for patients with dMMR/MSI-H, IDH1 mutations, FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, BRAF V600E mutations, HER2 overexpression, RET, NTRK1/2/3, or NRG1 fusions.Additional information is available at https://ascopubs.org/guidelines/living-guidelines.

items.title: Surface-guided radiotherapy setup using an open-face mask for head and neck cancer; the OPEN trial approach
items.authors: Ryan S, Fitzpatrick C, Malone C, et al.
items.abstract: Head and neck (H&N) radiotherapy requires reproducible immobilisation to maintain geometric accuracy; however, conventional thermoplastic masks are associated with patient discomfort and anxiety. Surface-guided radiotherapy (SGRT) provides non-ionising, real-time guidance for patient positioning and intrafraction monitoring from setup through to treatment completion. However, its application in H&N radiotherapy requires careful consideration of the complex and independently mobile anatomy of the face, neck and shoulders. This MethodsX protocol accompanies the OPEN Phase III randomised control trial and describes the technical and clinical workflow for the SGRT-supported open-face immobilisation arms. It provides a reproducible framework for centres seeking to implement the OPEN approach.•Initial alignment is performed using SGRT postural video guidance based on the patient's external contour.•A facial setup ROI is used for head positioning.•A larger monitoring ROI encompassing the face, neck and upper thorax is then used to refine lower neck and shoulder position while maintaining facial alignment, and for continuous intrafraction monitoring during treatment.The OPEN trial demonstrated that this workflow maintained setup accuracy, intrafraction stability and clinical efficiency while supporting open-face immobilisation. This companion protocol provides the practical detail required to reproduce the workflow in clinical practice.

items.title: Global Landscape of Clinical Studies Open to Enrollment in Carbon Ion Radiotherapy: A PTCOG Review
items.authors: Holtzman AL, Giap H, Ishikawa H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radiotherapy with high linear energy transfer (LET) has shown promise for improving cancer outcomes. Carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) combines charged-particle dose conformality with enhanced biological effectiveness. However, clinical development remains constrained by limited center availability, modest trial accrual, and few randomized studies. We reviewed the global landscape of CIRT studies open to enrollment to identify current priorities and gaps. Methods: This Particle Therapy Cooperative Group (PTCOG)-sanctioned project, conducted within the CIRT Guidelines Subcommittee, identified studies through registry review and institutional verification. ClinicalTrials.gov and the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials were searched from December 2025 through February 2026. We included interventional CIRT trials and prospective registries open to new enrollment and excluded studies not open to enrollment, retrospective cohorts, proton-only studies, and preclinical studies. Results: Thirty-six studies were identified: 35 interventional trials in 6 countries and 1 North American registry-based comparative-effectiveness study. Japan had the largest share, followed by Germany, China, Italy, Austria, and France. Three centers (SPHIC, QST, and HIT) accounted for 21 of 36 studies. The portfolio included 7 phase I, 23 phase II, 5 phase III, and 1 registry study. Pancreatic cancer and sarcoma-related tumors each accounted for 7 studies; head and neck cancers, 5; prostate and breast cancers, 3 each; glioblastoma, lung cancer, and gynecologic malignancies, 2 each; and mucosal melanoma, mixed solid tumors, kidney cancer, esophageal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, 1 each. Most studies were conducted at a single institution and emphasized feasibility, toxicity, local control, progression-free survival, or overall survival. Conclusions: This expert-verified inventory shows that CIRT studies open to enrollment remain concentrated by center, disease site, and phase. Future progress may depend more on shared outcome definitions, transparent biological dose reporting, and registry-enabled or multicenter comparative designs than on additional isolated single-institution studies.

items.title: Neoadjuvant Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Before Inferior Vena Cava Thrombectomy for Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Hannan R, Lin L, Assadi R, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with inferior vena cava (IVC) tumor thrombus is associated with substantial perioperative risk and frequent recurrence despite nephrectomy and thrombectomy. No established neoadjuvant local therapy exists for this high-risk population. Objective: To evaluate the feasibility, safety, clinical outcomes, and exploratory biomarker effects of neoadjuvant stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) targeting IVC tumor thrombus before nephrectomy and thrombectomy. Design, Setting, And Participants: This single-center prospective phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with newly diagnosed RCC and Mayo level II to IV IVC tumor thrombus eligible for neoadjuvant SABR and definitive surgery from July 2015 to January 2024. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to August 2026. Intervention: Neoadjuvant SABR to the radiographically defined IVC tumor thrombus, delivered as 40 Gy in 5 fractions or 36 Gy in 3 fractions, followed by radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary end point was 1-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) compared with a prespecified historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7%. Secondary outcomes included 90-day perioperative morbidity and mortality, adverse events, pulmonary embolism, overall survival, and cancer-specific survival. Exploratory analyses included Ki-67 immunohistochemistry and tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA. Results: Of 23 patients who received neoadjuvant SABR, 22 completed surgery, and 21 were included in the primary RFS analysis. Of 21 included patients, 12 (57%) were male, and the median (IQR) age was 62.5 (54.0-73.2) years. A total of 19 patients had clear-cell RCC; all tumors were grade 3 or 4, and 3 patients had metastatic disease at enrollment. At a median (range) follow-up of 108.6 (2.0-127.2) months, 1-year RFS was 71.4% (80% CI, 56.6-82.0; 95% CI, 47.2-86.0), meeting the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion based on comparison with the historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7% (P = .09). One-year overall survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3) and cancer-specific survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3). No 90-day perioperative mortality occurred; 4 grade 4 treatment-attributed events occurred, but no grade 4/5 radiation-attributed toxic effects occurred. Ki-67 expression was reduced in patients with irradiated tumor thrombus compared with nonirradiated controls. Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA was detected in all patients with available plasma and declined after treatment.…

items.title: (177)Lu-Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Prior to Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy in Oligorecurrent Prostate Cancer: Secondary and Exploratory End Point Results from the Randomized Phase 2 LUNAR Trial
items.authors: Kishan AU, Wilhalme H, Felix C, et al.
items.abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23-0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34-0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08-1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02-1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19-1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT-detected recurrence.

items.title: A Novel TCP and NTCP Modeling Framework Incorporating Inter-Fractional Deviations and Biological Effectiveness for Hyper-fractionated Radiotherapy
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Kong X, Fu X, Yu J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose. Methods And Materials: Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis. Results: Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. For grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis, the CBCT-based NTCP model achieved significantly higher AUC (0.67 vs. 0.59) and lower NLL (62.39 vs. 66.13) than that of the pCT-based mode. Superiority of CBCT-based NTCP model was also observed for grade ≥3 radiation esophagitis, i.e., AUC (0.62 vs. 0.58) and NLL (55.55 vs. 56.64). Using the observed LPFS as reference, marginally improved TCP modeling was observed using CBCT dose than that of pCT, where the AUC values were 0.80 vs. 0.79 (GTV 45 Gy) and 0.77 vs. 0.75 (GTV 54 Gy). Conclusions: By incorporating inter-fractional deviation and biological effectiveness, the improved accuracy of TCP and NTCP models provides preliminary evidence supporting the treatment planning and toxicity management for LS-SCLC patients treated with the hyper-fractionated radiotherapy, which needs further clinical validation.

items.title: Modern brachytherapy modalities vs. external beam radiotherapy in post-operative non-melanoma skin cancer: A systematic review
items.authors: Angeline WK, Hendriyo, Rudiyo, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Facial non-melanoma skin cancers (NMSCs) are primarily managed surgically, but adjuvant or definitive radiotherapy is indicated for high-risk or anatomically complex lesions. While electron-based external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) remains standard, high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy modalities now utilize surface moulds, 3D-printed applicators, interstitial implants, and flap techniques. This systematic review assessed the oncological efficacy, dosimetric characteristics, toxicity, and cosmetic outcomes of these brachytherapy techniques compared with EBRT. Material And Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, Springer, and Wiley Online Library for studies evaluating modern brachytherapy and EBRT in NMSC. Data on local control (LC), cosmesis, organ preservation, and toxicity were extracted and synthesized. Results: Twenty-three studies met the inclusion criteria. Modern brachytherapy achieved local control rates of 90% to 100%, demonstrating clinical non-inferiority to EBRT. Brachytherapy exhibited a steeper dose fall-off than EBRT, facilitating target volume dose delivery while sparing adjacent organs at risk. This advantage resulted in high rates of organ preservation, notably avoiding radiation-induced cataracts in periocular applications, and favorable clinician- and patient-reported cosmetic outcomes. Utilizing 3D-printing optimized applicator conformity, and eliminated air gaps in irregular anatomical topographies. Morbidity was primarily limited to transient grade 1 or 2 acute cutaneous reactions, with severe late toxicities below 2%. Conclusions: Modern HDR brachytherapy provides local control equivalent to EBRT, along with superior dosimetric conformity, functional preservation, and cosmetic outcomes. Its capacity for hypofractionation also offers an operational advantage. Treatment selection requires an individualized, multidisciplinary approach based on tumor depth, anatomical complexity, and institutional capability. Future multicenter randomized controlled trials incorporating standardized patient-reported outcomes are required to validate these findings.

items.title: Nivolumab-Ipilimumab for Localized Microsatellite Instability-High Gastric/Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma: The Phase 2 NEONIPIGA Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Samaille T, Henriques J, Tougeron D, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in localized deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma was evaluated in the NEONIPIGA study. The primary end point of pathological complete response (pCR) was previously reported. Objective: To report long-term follow-up results and secondary end points, including event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS), of the NEONIPIGA study. Design, Setting, And Participants: The NEONIPIGA study is a French, multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial that included patients with histologically proven cT2-T4NXM0 deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability-high GEJ adenocarcinoma who were eligible for surgery. Patients were enrolled between October 23, 2019, and June 4, 2021, and the database was locked on November 13, 2025. Intervention: Neoadjuvant nivolumab, 240 mg, every 2 weeks for 6 cycles plus ipilimumab, 1 mg/kg, every 6 weeks for 2 cycles, followed by surgery 5 weeks after the last nivolumab dose, and adjuvant nivolumab, 480 mg, every 4 weeks for 9 cycles. Main Outcomes And Measures: EFS and OS. Results: A total of 32 patients (median [range] age, 65 [40-80] years; 8 [28%] female and 21 [72%] were male) were included: 16 (50%) with gastric cancer and 16 (50%) with GEJ cancer. Three patients did not undergo surgery (1 with metastatic disease and 2 who refused). Twenty-seven patients (84%) completed neoadjuvant therapy and 14 (44%) received all treatment as planned. Neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 6 (19%) and 4 patients (17%), respectively. Median follow-up was 48.3 months (95% CI, 44.8-52.0 months). Among the 32 patients in the intention-to-treat population, 4-year OS was 84.1% (95% CI, 65.8%-93.0%). In the 31 patients eligible for surgery, 4-year EFS was 83.5% (95% CI, 64.8%-92.8%). One patient relapsed with cerebral metastases. Six deaths occurred: 2 related to gastric cancer or treatment (1 patient had postoperative complications and 1 cerebral metastases) and 4 unrelated. All patients who did not undergo surgery achieved a clinical complete response after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. One patient subsequently died of causes unrelated to their cancer. Overall, 17 of 29 patients (59%) achieved pCR on surgical specimen. Safety was previously reported, and no additional late toxic effects were observed.…

items.title: Machine Learning Models Combining [(68)Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET Radiomics and Clinical Features to Predict Overall Survival for Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer Treated with [(177)Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligand Therapy
items.authors: Edouard L, Papillon L, Ferrer L, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains incurable despite recent therapeutic advances. [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (lutetium-177 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy) provides meaningful clinical benefit in selected patients. However, ∼30% of the patients do not respond to [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Although several baseline prognostic factors are well known, reliable pretherapeutic predictive biomarkers are still lacking. We developed and compared several predictive machine learning (ML) models integrating clinical, biochemical, and imaging data, including [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET (gallium-68 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen ligand positron emission tomography) radiomic features, to estimate overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Methods: This retrospective monocentric study included 102 patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA between January 2022 and March 2024. Five lesions per patient were segmented on their pretherapeutic [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/computed tomography (CT) scans. Radiomic features were extracted following Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative guidelines. Multimodal ML models integrating clinical, genomic, biochemical, and imaging features (including radiomics) were developed to predict OS. Results: Median OS of the total cohort was 11.2 mo. Intralesional homogeneity, characterized by the second-order radiomic feature normalized inverse difference moment, was associated with shorter OS (p = 0.025). The best-performing ML model achieved a 12-mo area under the curve (AUC) of 0.778 by combining 22 clinical, biochemical, genomic, and radiomic features. The model leveraging PET data alone achieved strong performance, with an AUC comparable to the clinical model (0.715 vs 0.766). Conclusions: ML models based on [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, including radiomic features, offer a noninvasive, standardized, and widely accessible approach to predict OS in patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. This study highlights the strong predictive potential of PSMA PET imaging for patient stratification in a real-world setting.

items.title: US-based Delphi Consensus Study on Adjuvant Radiation Therapy (ART) in Node-Negative Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC)
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Stevens JS, Barker CA, Bakst RL, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: There is a paucity of high-level evidence for adjuvant radiation therapy (ART) in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) creating practice variations. This study provides expert consensus recommendations on patient and tumor selection, timing, duration, dosage, and additional considerations for ART in node-negative CSCC. Methods: The Delphi panel included 35 experts in radiation oncology (15), dermatology/Mohs micrographic surgery (9), medical oncology (7), head and neck surgery (3), and surgical oncology (1). Consensus was defined as ≥80% concordance; near-consensus 70-79% concordance. Results: Consensus was reached to recommend ART when further surgery is not possible, but the tumor has positive gross or histologic/microscopic margins (35/35, 100%). Key consensus or near-consensus recommendations for recommending ART to the tumor bed following negative-margin surgery include: 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence (29/35, 83%) or nodal metastasis (27/35, 77%) ≥ 20%; gross cortical bone/marrow invasion (32/35, 91%); skull base invasion (32/35, 91%); 4 risk factors (RF) (35/35, 100%); 3 RF (30-33/35, 86-94%); PNI ≥ 0.1 mm and one other RF (30/35, 86%); and clinical nerve invasion (31/35, 89%). Immune status influenced ART decision-making (30/35, 86%) with 77% (27/35) more likely to recommend ART for immunosuppressed patients. Consensus was reached to omit ART for pathologic complete response following neoadjuvant immunotherapy (34/35, 97%). Among radiation oncologists, 100% (15/15) agreed the optimal window for ART to the tumor bed is 4-8 weeks and that hypofractionated regimens can be appropriate (12/15, 80%). Consensus was reached for prescription doses of 60-66 Gy in 2 Gy/fx (15/15, 100%) or 50-55 Gy in 2.5 Gy/fx (13/15, 87%), and that superficial radiation and brachytherapy are inappropriate ART modalities for node-negative high-stage CSCC (14/15, 93%). There was no consensus on elective nodal basin irradiation. Conclusions: This Delphi study provides an expert consensus-based framework to standardize ART for node-negative high-stage CSCC following surgery, informing future guidelines and utilization.

items.title: Organ Preservation and Quality of Life After Total Neoadjuvant Treatment in Rectal Cancer
items.authors: Diefenhardt M, Fokas E, Kosmala R, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Data on quality of life (QOL) after total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) are important for counseling patients on the benefits of watch-and-wait (WW) vs total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer. A thorough understanding of both options and their long-term impact on bowel, urinary, sexual function, and other QOL domains remains limited. Objective: To examine the association of organ preservation with QOL and functional outcomes among patients with rectal cancer treated in 2 phase 2 clinical trials. Design, Setting, And Participants: This unplanned, post hoc, cohort study used data from the CAO/ARO/AIO-12 and CAO/ARO/AIO-16 trials, recruiting participants from June 15, 2015, through October 7, 2020, from 19 centers in Germany. Included patients had cT3 to cT4 or node-positive rectal adenocarcinoma. Total neoadjuvant treatment included chemoradiation therapy combined with induction or consolidation chemotherapy. The statistical analysis was performed from March 6 to December 23, 2025. Main Outcomes And Measures: The association of WW with functional outcomes and QOL was assessed using prospectively recorded EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-CR29, and Wexner score questionnaires. Differences in QOL scores were estimated using adjusted longitudinal and cross-sectional analyses with a predefined clinically meaningful difference of at least 5 points. Results: Baseline questionnaires were available from 346 of 385 eligible patients (89.9%; median [range] age, 60 [19-80] years; 257 male [67%]), while available QOL questionnaires decreased over time to 185 (48.1%) at 5 years. Using the longitudinal analytic approach, statistically significant and clinically meaningful differences in favor of WW were noted for fecal incontinence (-21.2 [95% CI, -30.0 to -12.3]; P < .001); stool frequency (-19.8 [95% CI, -27.6 to -11.9]; P < .001); embarrassment (-17.0 [95% CI, -27.4 to -6.6]; P = .002); flatulence (-15.2 [95% CI, -24.4 to -6.0]; P < .001), buttock pain (-11.9 [95% CI, -20.8 to -3.0]; P = .01); social (9.7 [95% CI, 1.1-18.3]; P = .03), physical (10.2 [95% CI, 4.1-16.3]; P = .002), and role (13.9 [95% CI, 4.9-22.9]; P = .003) functioning; and global health status (9.2 [95% CI, 3.2-15.2]; P = .004). These clinically meaningful differences were detectable in both the intended organ preservation and disease-free groups.…

items.title: The relationship between endometrial cancer and urinary incontinence: systematic review
items.authors: Mohammed Ali Al Saleh F, Ibrahim Bograin K, Saud Alaqil A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The most common gynecological cancer in industrialized countries is endometrial cancer (EC), whose prevalence is growing and is associated with metabolic syndrome and obesity. Women's quality of life is negatively impacted by the common and upsetting disorder known as urinary incontinence (UI), particularly in postmenopausal and post-surgical populations. Despite plausible biological and iatrogenic connections between EC and UI-including shared risk factors such as obesity and the impact of hysterectomy on pelvic anatomy-the relationship remains inadequately synthesized in the literature. Objective: The purpose of this systematic review is to summarize the data about the connection between endometrial cancer and incontinence, looking at prevalence, potential etiological mechanisms, and implications for clinical care. Methods: A comprehensive search for English-language studies published in the last ten years was done using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. MeSH phrases and keywords associated with urinary incontinence and endometrial cancer were used in the search. Two reviewers used Rayyan software to independently pick studies, extract data, and evaluate quality. Because the studies were so different from one another, a narrative synthesis technique was used. Results: Six studies comprising 955 patients and 85 healthcare professionals met inclusion criteria. The collective evidence reveals that UI is a highly prevalent yet often undermanaged consequence of EC and its treatments. Findings demonstrate that lymph node dissection may contribute to urinary symptoms, though not reaching statistical significance. Radiotherapy exhibits paradoxical effects-potentially improving stress UI while contributing to broader pelvic floor dysfunction through radiation-induced fibrosis and measurable alterations in pelvic floor muscle properties. Obesity and age, rather than radiation exposure consistently, become important risk factors on their own. Conclusion: Due to common risk factors, direct effects of the disease, and damage from therapy, urinary incontinence is a common and clinically important side effect of endometrial cancer and its therapies. As the number of EC survivors keeps rising, addressing UI must become a priority in comprehensive survivorship care. Future efforts should focus on developing validated screening tools, establishing evidence-based management guidelines, and implementing integrated care models.

items.title: Randomized Trial of Hypofractionated Postmastectomy Radiation Therapy in Women With Breast Reconstruction (RT CHARM, Alliance A221505)
items.authors: Poppe MM, Le-Rademacher JJ, Haffty BG, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Patients with breast cancer requiring postmastectomy radiation therapy (PMRT) often desire breast reconstruction. Reconstructions can be adversely affected by PMRT, and fear of reconstruction complications has discouraged adoption of short-course radiation therapy used after lumpectomy. To fill the evidence gap, we conducted a noninferiority trial of hypofractionated versus conventional PMRT in patients undergoing breast reconstruction. The primary outcome was reconstruction complication rate, a composite of wound healing, readmission, capsular contracture, unplanned reoperation, and reconstruction failure. Methods: Women with unilateral invasive breast cancer with planned immediate or delayed reconstruction and PMRT were randomly assigned (1:1) to 50 Gy (25 fractions/5 weeks) or 42.56 Gy (16 fractions/3 weeks). This study was designed with a noninferiority margin of 10%, assuming a 2-year reconstruction complication rate of 25% with conventional PMRT. Randomization was stratified by immediate versus delayed and autologous versus implant-only reconstruction. Results: Between 2018 and 2021, 898 patients enrolled with a median follow-up of 3.9 years; 825 patients were evaluable for the primary end point. The 24-month reconstruction complication rates were 12.3% (52/422) with hypofractionated PMRT and 10.2% (41/403) with conventional PMRT, corresponding to an estimated difference of -2.1% (95% CI, -6.5 to 2.2). The complication rate was higher (regardless of arm) with implant-only versus autologous reconstruction (odds ratio = 1.65). There was no statistically significant difference in 36-month locoregional recurrence rates: 1.5% (95% CI, 0.7 to 3.2) with hypofractionated and 2.2% (95% CI, 1.1 to 4.3) with conventional PMRT. Acute and late toxicity rates were not statistically different. Conclusion: A 16-fraction course of hypofractionated PMRT is safe and noninferior to conventional PMRT in women undergoing breast reconstruction after mastectomy.

items.title: Initial complete local therapy without systemic therapy versus systemic-therapy-based management in selected patients with oligometastatic renal cell carcinoma: a matched comparative study
items.authors: Kim HU, Lee HI, Park I, et al.
items.abstract: Objectives: To compare survival outcomes of initial complete metastasis-directed therapy (MDT) without systemic therapy (ST) and ST-based management in patients with oligometastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Materials And Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients with oligometastatic RCC (≤5 lesions) treated between 2015 and 2023. Patients were categorized as MDT alone (surgery, radiotherapy, or both, without ST) or ST ± local treatment. One-to-one exact matching between the initial MDT-alone and ST-based groups was performed using six covariates (lesion count, timing of presentation, IMDC risk, Charlson comorbidity index, number of involved organs, and performance status). Results: Among 276 patients (MDT, n = 173; ST, n = 103), 72 pairs were generated after exact matching. Median follow-up was 86.2 months for the MDT and 71.6 months for the ST group in the matched cohort. MDT alone was associated with higher 5-year overall survival (OS) (73.0 % vs. 58.6 %; hazard ratio [HR] 0.45, 95 % confidence interval [CI] 0.26-0.77, p = 0.004) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) (83.7 % vs. 69.8 %; HR 0.35, 95 % CI 0.18-0.67; p = 0.001) in the matched cohort. Progression-free survival (PFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) did not differ between groups. In the MDT alone group, the 5-year cumulative incidence of subsequent ST initiation was 48.6 %. In the whole cohort, the association was consistent across IMDC risk groups (p-interaction = 0.898). Conclusions: In this selected post-nephrectomy cohort, an initial complete-local-therapy strategy without ST was associated with higher OS and CSS than heterogeneous, predominantly TKI-based ST management, although PFS and DMFS were similar. Given the nonrandomized treatment allocation and residual biological selection, these findings are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as evidence of superiority over contemporary ICI-based therapy.

items.title: First-In-Human Study of (211)At-CD45 Radioimmunotherapy With Nonmyeloablative Conditioning Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Adults With Hematologic Malignancies
items.authors: Vo PT, Walter RB, Gooley TA, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Relapse is the dominant cause of failure after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) for aggressive hematologic malignancies. CD45-directed radioimmunotherapy (RIT) has been investigated to intensify conditioning and augment antitumor efficacy. After gaining clinical experience with β-emitting radionuclides, attention is now shifting toward α-emitters, such as astatine-211 (211At), for their more potent and precise radiation delivery with minimized toxicity to surrounding tissues. Patients And Methods: To our knowledge, in this first-in-human, two-stage dose-finding study, we administered a single infusion of 211At-labeled anti-CD45 monoclonal antibody before nonmyeloablative conditioning with fludarabine/2-3 Gy total body irradiation and allografting from HLA-matched or single-allele-mismatched donors in 45 adults (38-74 years of age) at a high relapse risk from myeloid malignancies or acute leukemia. Results: Seventeen patients were treated in stage I with 85-591 μCi/kg of 211At. The patient receiving 591 μCi/kg developed veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD/SOS), thereby establishing 500 μCi/kg as the protocol-defined maximum tolerated dose and prompting initiation of stage II at that dose in 28 patients. Infusion reactions were mild. 211At-CD45 RIT did not delay hematopoietic recovery, impair donor chimerism, or increase graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) rates. In stage II, six patients (all receiving sirolimus as part of GVHD prophylaxis for unrelated donor HCT) experienced VOD/SOS. Among the 13 patients with circulating blasts at baseline, blasts cleared in 12 before initiation of fludarabine/total body irradiation, demonstrating immediate cytotoxic activity. Estimated 1-year relapse-free and overall survival were 42% (95% CI, 28%-56%) and 49% (34%-62%), respectively. Conclusion: 211At-CD45 RIT can be incorporated into nonmyeloablative conditioning, with liver toxicity defining activity limits. Evidence of antitumor efficacy supports phase II evaluation.

items.title: Five-Year Late Toxicity After Ultra-Hypofractionated Whole-Breast Radiotherapy With Simultaneous Integrated Boost: A Prospective Multicentre Cohort Study
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Dzhugashvili M, Lopez E, Fernández-Ibiza J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Ultra-hypofractionated whole-breast radiotherapy has become an accepted option for early breast cancer, but evidence on the incorporation of a simultaneous integrated boost within a five-fraction schedule remains limited. The present study evaluated five-year late side effects after whole-breast irradiation with a simultaneous integrated boost delivered in five fractions in a prospective multicentre cohort. Methods: This prospective, non-randomized, multicentre cohort included 242 patients with early breast cancer treated between April and December 2020. All patients underwent breast-conserving surgery with clear margins. Whole-breast irradiation was delivered at 26 Gy in five daily fractions, and 157 patients received a simultaneous integrated boost to 29 Gy in five fractions. The primary endpoint was late normal-tissue side effects in the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, assessed prospectively with clinical examination, photographic documentation, and LENT-SOMA scoring. Comparisons with patients treated without a boost were exploratory. Results: Median follow-up was 64.7 months in both the overall cohort and the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, and 221 of 242 patients completed the scheduled five-year visit. In the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, cumulative any-grade pain was reported in 14.6% of patients at five years, and cumulative any-grade fibrosis in 8.9%. Other late side effects were uncommon, including breast oedema in 5.1%, arm oedema in 0.6%, atrophy in 1.9%, and telangiectasia in 0.6%; no ulceration was observed. In exploratory unadjusted analyses, pain was more frequent in the simultaneous integrated boost group than in the no-boost group, whereas no significant differences were observed for other late side effects. Chemotherapy receipt was also associated with persistent pain in exploratory analyses. Conclusions: Whole-breast irradiation with a 29 Gy simultaneous integrated boost in five fractions achieved low rates of objective late side effects and reassuring oncological outcomes after more than five years, while shortening treatment to a single one-week course compared with sequential or moderately hypofractionated schedules. Persistent low-grade breast pain was more frequent with the boost, but non-randomized allocation and its association with chemotherapy preclude causal attribution, supporting continued, careful use in selected patients alongside further prospective, randomized studies with baseline symptom assessment.

items.title: Unilateral vs Bilateral Hippocampal Avoidance During WBRT With Memantine for Brain Metastases: A Randomized Single-Blind Phase 2 Clinical Trial
items.authors: Yang WC, Chen YF, Yang CC, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Hippocampal avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy (HA-WBRT) with memantine reduces, but does not eliminate, cognitive decline. Left hippocampal dose may be more closely associated with cognitive outcomes. We investigated whether unilateral (left) HA-WBRT is equivalent to bilateral HA-WBRT for neurocognitive function. Methods In this randomized, single-blind, phase 2 equivalence trial, patients with brain metastases were assigned 1:1 to unilateral (left) or bilateral HA-WBRT (30 Gy in 10 fractions) with concurrent memantine. The primary endpoint was relative decline in Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R) memory score from baseline to 6 months; equivalence required the 90% CI for the between-arm difference to fall within ±15 percentage points. Results Among 73 patients (unilateral, n = 36; bilateral, n = 37; median follow-up, 13.2 months), mean 6-month relative HVLT-R decline was 4.75% versus 5.05% (difference, -0.31%; 90% CI, -12.02% to 11.40%; TOST P = .02), meeting the equivalence criterion. Brain progression-free survival (10.3 vs 10.8 months; P = .96), overall survival (17.8 vs 12.8 months; P = .94), acute toxicity (≥ grade 2, 44.4% vs 35.1%; P = .43), and 6-month neurocognitive failure (61.1% vs 56.8%; Gray test P = .78) were similar. Global health status appeared more stable with unilateral HA-WBRT (interaction, P < .001). Exploratory plasma BDNF trajectories varied by neurocognitive failure status (FDR q = .09). Conclusions Unilateral (left) HA-WBRT with memantine met the prespecified equivalence criterion for verbal memory, with comparable oncologic outcomes and safety; non-verbal memory was not assessed. These findings warrant validation, particularly when bilateral avoidance is challenging.

items.title: Interventional radiation immune-boosting (iRIB). The role of concomitant interventional radiotherapy (modern brachytherapy) in immunotherapy: A hypothesis-generating systematic review
items.authors: Muni R, Lancellotta V, Fionda B, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Synergistic activity of radiation and immunotherapy is well known to the extent that it can be referred to as radiation immuno-boosting. Interventional radiotherapy (IRT; modern brachytherapy) has a potential immunomodulatory advantage compared with external beam radiotherapy due to highly conformal dose distribution and dose heterogeneity, engaging multiple immunogenic mechanisms with distinct dose-response profiles. Material And Methods: A hypothesis-generating systematic review was conducted in June 2026 using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases to identify clinical studies reporting outcomes of patients treated with IRT plus immunotherapy, including any primary tumor, assessing efficacy and toxicity. Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using a GRADE-based approach. Among the identified publications, 13 studies were included in qualitative synthesis. Results: The included studies published between 2019 and 2026 were non-randomized, and comprised 98 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, melanoma, kidney, and pancreatic or lung cancer. IRT was delivered before, concurrently, or in close temporal proximity to immunotherapy. Radiological tumor response of irradiated lesions was consistently reported, although outcome definitions were heterogeneous and often descriptive. Progression-free survival ranged from 1 to over 30 months. Severe treatment-related toxicity (grade ≥ 3) was uncommon, and no unexpected safety signals were observed. Occasional regression of non-irradiated lesions was reported; however, these observations were anecdotal and cannot be reliably attributed to radiation-induced systemic immune activation. Conclusions: Interventional radiotherapy has a biological rationale for potential immunomodulatory interactions with immunotherapy, but these effects have not yet been established clinically. Although current clinical evidence is limited and of very low certainty, preliminary findings support additional prospective investigation. Further prospective studies are required to better characterize the optimal integration of IRT and immunotherapy, including radiation dose, fractionation schedules, and treatment sequencing.

items.title: A Randomized Phase III Trial of Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy Followed by Durvalumab Consolidation, With or Without Induction Chemo-Immunotherapy, in Patients With Unresectable Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: JCOG2510 (PRIME-CRT)
items.authors: Kawabata K, Masuda K, Miura K, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) followed by durvalumab consolidation is the current standard of care for unresectable locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC). However, survival outcomes in this setting remain unsatisfactory. Although the PACIFIC trial improved outcomes, further intensification of systemic therapy may be required to improve long-term survival. Preclinical and perioperative clinical evidence suggests that introducing immunotherapy in the presence of an intact primary tumor may enhance antitumor immune responses. Recently, early-phase studies have reported the feasibility and potential efficacy of induction chemo-immunotherapy followed by cCRT; however, its clinical benefit has not been confirmed in a phase III trial. Patients And Methods: This multicenter, randomized, phase III trial is designed to determine whether the addition of induction chemo-immunotherapy to the current standard strategy of cCRT followed by durvalumab consolidation improves survival outcomes in patients with unresectable LA-NSCLC. Previously untreated patients with unresectable LA-NSCLC without activating EGFR mutations are randomized 1:1 to receive either cCRT followed by durvalumab consolidation or induction chemo-immunotherapy followed by cCRT and durvalumab consolidation. Randomization is adjusted for age, clinical stage, programmed death-ligand 1 expression, and institution. The primary endpoints are progression-free and overall survival. Secondary endpoints include objective response rate, proportion of patients proceeding to cCRT after induction therapy, and adverse events. A total of 212 patients will be enrolled from 60 institutions over 5 years. Conclusion: The results of this trial should clarify whether the addition of induction chemo-immunotherapy can enhance curative potential and lead to improved overall survival in patients with unresectable LA-NSCLC.

items.title: Adjuvant radiotherapy in FIGO stage III dMMR endometrial cancer: evidence and perspectives in the molecular era
items.authors: Macchia G, Merlotti A, De Felice F, et al.
items.abstract: Current guidelines incorporate chemo-immunotherapy for stage III-IV mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) endometrial cancer, but the evidence supporting omission of adjuvant radiotherapy remains insufficient. Given the pivotal role of pelvic radiotherapy in achieving durable locoregional control in high-risk endometrial cancer, and the lack of robust randomized evidence demonstrating equivalence of systemic therapy alone, the suggestion that EBRT may be safely omitted in the adjuvant treatment of dMMR high-risk disease warrants careful consideration. Importantly, PORTEC-3 (NCT00411138) included radiotherapy in both treatment groups and no immunotherapy, whereas in KEYNOTE-B21 (ENGOT-en11/GOG-3053, NCT04634877) radiotherapy was not randomized; neither trial therefore directly tested the safety of radiotherapy omission. In this Viewpoint, we review current evidence and unresolved questions in the adjuvant management of FIGO stage III dMMR endometrial cancer, with particular attention to the role of radiotherapy in the evolving chemo-immunotherapy era. While our discussion is intentionally focused on dMMR disease, many of the broader considerations regarding the interpretation of emerging evidence and the preservation of effective locoregional treatment are not exclusive to this molecular subgroup. Ongoing trials, including NRG-GY020 (NCT04214067) and the RAINBO MMRd-GREEN trial (ENGOT-en14/GREEN, NCT05255653), are expected to define the optimal integration of immunotherapy and adjuvant radiotherapy in molecularly stratified populations. Beyond survival, locoregional control, recurrence burden, and quality of life remain clinically meaningful endpoints. Future randomized trials should evaluate radiotherapy as an independent treatment variable within molecularly stratified populations, incorporating not only survival but also patterns of failure and patient-reported outcomes. Until such data become available, treatment de-escalation strategies should be adopted with caution.

items.title: Uncertainty quantification for detecting out-of-distribution cases in deep learning segmentation of head and neck organs of interest
items.authors: van Aalst JE, Simões R, Maruccio FC, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Quality assurance (QA) of auto-segmentations is necessary for safe clinical deployment. Deep learning models are optimised for data similar to their training set, but reliability drops with out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. This study evaluates whether uncertainty quantification (UQ) can detect OOD inputs arising from distribution shift in head and neck organ of interest (OOI) auto-segmentation. Materials And Methods: Monte Carlo dropout-based uncertainty scores and geometric accuracy of nnU-Net models were evaluated in two experiments. First, as a proof-of-concept, we assessed whether uncertainty scores detect metal artefact (N = 10) from non-artefact cases (N = 10) on a baseline model (mixed training data, N = 620) and a no-metal model (artefact-free training data, N = 620). Second, in a clinically realistic experiment, we split a fine-tuning dataset by uncertainty score to obtain a narrow model (low-uncertainty cases, N = 21) and a broad model (high-uncertainty cases, N = 21). A held-out test set (N = 76) evaluated whether segmentation accuracy differed between uncertainty categories. Results: Both experiments showed that uncertainty scores reflect the learned training distribution. In the supervised experiment, the no-metal model demonstrated greater uncertainty score separation between artefact and non-artefact cases (1.1 × 105 vs 0.6 × 105) than the baseline model (1.1 × 105 vs 0.8 × 105). In the unsupervised experiment, the narrow model performed significantly better on certain than uncertain cases (p = 0.04), while no difference was seen for the broad model (p = 0.34), which did include these cases in training. Conclusions: Uncertainty quantification can detect distribution shifts in radiotherapy auto-segmentation. This could support automated QA workflows by identifying in-distribution cases and enabling the application of specialised models.

items.title: VERIFY: A Phase III Trial of Rusfertide Versus Placebo in Phlebotomy-Dependent Patients With Polycythemia Vera Receiving Standard-of-Care Therapy
items.authors: Kuykendall AT, Bankar A, Pettit KM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by erythrocytosis. Rusfertide is a subcutaneous, injectable, hepcidin mimetic peptide that suppresses erythrocytosis. The phase III VERIFY trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of rusfertide in phlebotomy-dependent patients with PV and poorly controlled hematocrit. Methods: In VERIFY Part 1a (32 weeks), patients requiring frequent phlebotomy were randomly assigned (1:1, double-blind) to receive rusfertide or placebo with or without cytoreductive therapy. The primary efficacy end point was clinical response (absence of phlebotomy eligibility; weeks 20-32). Key secondary end points (baseline to week 32) included mean number of phlebotomies, proportion of patients who maintained hematocrit <45%, and mean change from baseline in patient-reported outcomes (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System [PROMIS] Fatigue Short Form 8a [SF-8a] T score and Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form [MFSAF] Total Symptom Score-7 items [TSS7]). Results: Patients (N = 293) were randomly assigned to rusfertide (n = 147) or placebo (n = 146). Significantly more patients (n = 113, 77%) achieved a clinical response with rusfertide versus placebo (n = 48; 33%; P < .0001). Compared with placebo, rusfertide reduced mean ± standard deviation number of phlebotomies (0.5 ± 1.2 v 1.8 ± 1.5; P < .0001) and was superior in maintaining hematocrit <45% (n = 92 [63%] v n = 21 [14%]; P < .0001). Rusfertide led to a significant improvement in the PROMIS Fatigue SF-8a T-score and MFSAF TSS7 versus placebo (P = .0252 and .0240, respectively). Injection site reactions, anemia, and fatigue were the most common adverse events. No deaths were reported. Conclusion: Rusfertide significantly improved hematocrit control, reduced the need for phlebotomy, and improved patient-reported symptoms versus placebo in phlebotomy-dependent patients with PV who were also receiving standard-of-care therapy.

items.title: Deep learning-based spot weight generation for online adaptive IMPT: implementation and technical feasibility on a clinical delivery system
items.authors: Pang B, Quan H, Li T, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To investigate the feasibility of a deep learning-based method for generating intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) spot weights to enable a faster, more automated workflow. Methods: A 3D Attention U-Net with a masked mean absolute error loss generated spot weights from four input channels (optimized plan dose, reference dose, CT image, spot mask), using planned spot weights as labels, and trained and tested on prostate, brain, and lung cases. Robustness was evaluated on target dose metrics only. The workflow was validated in the Eclipse® treatment planning system and delivered on a ProBeam 360° system. Results: For weights in the range 0-5, mean absolute errors were below 0.8 for the prostate and brain models (15.9% and 48.1% of all weights, respectively) and below 1.7 for the lung model (31.2%). Mean relative errors were below 10% for the prostate model (5-65, 83.7%), 20% for the brain model (5-65, 51.7%), and 40% for the lung model (5-110, 68.6%); the remaining weights lay above these ranges and accounted for <0.5% of all weights. Gamma passing rates within the body contours (2%, 2 mm, 10% dose threshold) were 99.73 ± 0.32%, 98.95 ± 0.86%, and 92.75 ± 3.52% for the prostate, brain, and lung models, respectively. All delivered plans met the clinical QA acceptance criteria. Conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates the technical feasibility of generating IMPT spot weights with deep learning and implementing them on a clinical delivery system. Further improvement is needed for heterogeneous sites such as the lung.

items.title: Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy as induction therapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy and camrelizumab consolidation in limited-stage small cell lung cancer: a randomized phase II trial
items.authors: Liu D, Yang L, Hu M, et al.
items.abstract: Definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by immunotherapy consolidation is the current standard of care for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC). We conducted a randomized phase II trial (ChiCTR2000032275) to evaluate a camrelizumab-based induction-consolidation strategy in previously untreated patients with LS-SCLC. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive induction camrelizumab plus etoposide-platinum followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and camrelizumab consolidation (camrelizumab group), or induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent CRT alone (cCRT group). The primary endpoint was the 1‑year progression‑free survival (PFS) rate. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Between November 2020 and April 2024, 41 patients were enrolled. At a median follow‑up of 32.1 months (interquartile range [IQR]: 26.4-38.7), ORR was 100% in the camrelizumab group and 83.3% in the cCRT group. The 1‑year PFS rates were 65.5% with camrelizumab versus 47.4% with cCRT (P = 0.029). Median PFS was 24.0 months versus 11.8 months, and median OS was not reached versus 23.9 months (P = 0.042). Exploratory biomarker analyses indicated that patients with lower baseline systemic inflammatory indices, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio <2.8 and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio <207.0, and those with a decline in lactate dehydrogenase at week 12 after CRT, derived greater benefit from camrelizumab. The OS benefit was also more evident in patients with Ki-67 ≤80%. Toxicities in the camrelizumab group were manageable, with a low incidence of severe immune-related adverse events (4.8%), and radiation pneumonitis rates were comparable between groups. Taken together, induction camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy, followed by CRT and camrelizumab consolidation, significantly improved survival outcomes in LS-SCLC, with a manageable safety profile, warranting further validation for this aggressive malignancy.

items.title: Talazoparib plus enzalutamide in high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer: a randomized phase 2 trial
items.authors: Zacchi F, Castro E, Imbach K, et al.
items.abstract: Combining inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase and androgen receptor (AR) pathway has demonstrated clinical activity in men with metastatic prostate cancer, although the extent of benefit in tumors lacking homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations remains uncertain. We conducted a randomized phase 2 trial evaluating talazoparib plus enzalutamide versus enzalutamide alone in men with high-volume metastatic hormone-naive prostate cancer (mHNPC). Fifty-four patients starting androgen deprivation therapy received two cycles of enzalutamide lead-in before 1:2 randomization to enzalutamide (n = 17) or enzalutamide plus talazoparib (n = 37). The primary endpoint was met, with a 73% prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <0.2 ng ml-1 response rate at 12 months in the combination arm (95% confidence interval (CI) = 56-86%), exceeding the prespecified efficacy threshold (P < 0.001); the PSA <0.2 rate in the control arm was 64.7% (95% CI = 38-86%, P = 0.54 for exploratory comparison between arms). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 68% patients receiving the combination versus 35% with enzalutamide alone, predominantly anemia (41%). Two fatal therapy-emergent myeloid neoplasms occurred in the enzalutamide plus talazoparib arm in patients with underlying genomic susceptibility. Analyses of paired tumor biopsies acquired at baseline and during enzalutamide lead-in phase demonstrated marked tumor transcriptional reprogramming after AR inhibition, including suppression of proliferation-associated and HRR-related gene expression programs, but without functional impairment of homologous recombination activity. Overall, talazoparib plus enzalutamide demonstrated clinical activity in patients with high-volume mHNPC but did not establish clear additional clinical benefit over enzalutamide alone in this biomarker-unselected population, while being associated with increased toxicity. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04332744 .

items.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Does Molecular Hydrogen Exert Radioprotective Effects Without Compromising the Antitumor Efficacy of Radiotherapy or Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy?
items.authors: Zhang YI, Miyakawa M, Miyakawa A
items.abstract: Radiotherapy and concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) are widely used for cancer treatment but are frequently associated with radiation-induced toxicities. Molecular hydrogen has been proposed as a potential radioprotective agent because it protects normal tissues from oxidative damage. However, an important concern is whether molecular hydrogen also protects tumor tissues. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate whether molecular hydrogen preserves tumor response while providing radioprotection in cancer patients receiving radiotherapy or CCRT. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed for conducting this review. Eligible studies were English-language original clinical studies of adult cancer patients (≥18 years) treated with radiotherapy or CCRT and receiving molecular hydrogen for radioprotection. Three electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science) were searched from inception to 8 July 2026. Seven studies involving 222 patients were qualitatively synthesized, of which 3 involving 130 patients were included in the meta-analysis. The random-effects model was used. The risk of bias was evaluated with validated tools. The risk ratio (RR) was used to estimate the pooled tumor response. Molecular hydrogen did not significantly affect tumor response compared with the control group (RR = 0.98, 95% CI 0.83-1.15). Sensitivity analysis restricted to randomized controlled trials yielded a broadly consistent result (RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.84-1.17). The narrative synthesis further indicated that molecular hydrogen reduced radiation-induced toxicities, improved quality of life, and did not adversely affect hematological parameters. In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that molecular hydrogen may have radioprotective effects in cancer patients receiving radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy, with the currently available evidence showing no significant reduction in tumor response. This review was registered with INPLASY (INPLASY202680108).

items.title: Deep learning-based metal artifact reduction in CT for head and neck radiotherapy
items.authors: Mihandoust E, Sheikhzadeh P, Lavasani SN, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Metal artifacts from dental fillings and implants compromise CT image quality, target delineation, and dose calculation accuracy in head and neck (H&N) radiotherapy. Previous reviews have largely focused on traditional metal artifact reduction methods and image quality metrics rather than radiotherapy-specific endpoints. This systematic review evaluates deep learning-based metal artifact reduction (DL-MAR) approaches for H&N radiotherapy, emphasizing technical advances and clinical dosimetric validation. Materials And Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus were systematically searched (updated April 2026) for studies assessing DL-MAR methods in H&N CT imaging and radiotherapy. Of 227 identified records, 40 studies (11 traditional MAR and 29 DL-MAR studies) met the inclusion criteria. Results: Reported DL architectures included convolutional neural networks, generative adversarial networks, dual-domain networks, diffusion models, and task-oriented loss functions. Among studies with clinical dosimetric validation, GAN-based and task-oriented approaches consistently reported dose deviations below 3%. Gamma pass rates exceeding 95% (3%/3 mm) were reported in a subset of these studies. Dual-domain and diffusion-based methods were evaluated primarily using image quality metrics without direct radiotherapy-specific dosimetric validation. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that DL-MAR may achieve clinically acceptable dosimetric accuracy while improving artifact suppression and target visualization in H&N radiotherapy planning. Task-oriented loss functions currently demonstrate promising potential for clinical translation based on available retrospective evidence. Broader clinical implementation remains limited by reliance on synthetic training data, restricted access to sinogram data, and the absence of prospective multicenter validation studies.

items.title: Experimentally derived beam quality correction factors for PPC05 and razor nano ionization chambers in proton scanned beams based on graphite calorimetry
items.authors: Gómez-Fernández N, Rossomme S, González-García E, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Ionization chamber based reference dosimetry of proton beam requires the use of beam quality correction factors which are obtained experimentally or by Monte Carlo simulation and are available to users in codes of practice and other publications. Purpose: The aim of this work is to determine experimental proton beam quality correction factors, k Q  , for two ionization chambers using a portable graphite calorimeter: the IBA reference-class PPC05 chamber and the IBA non reference-class Razor Nano chamber, using a portable graphite calorimeter. Methods: Measurements were performed in scanned clinical proton beams at two clinical centers. Absorbed dose to graphite was determined using a recently developed portable graphite calorimeter. The conversion factors for the absorbed dose to water determination were obtained by Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, the experimental k Q  factors were obtained by comparing ionization chamber readings with the calorimeter, measured using the same conditions, in terms of absorbed dose to water. Results: For the IBA PPC05 chamber, the experimental values agreed with recommended values tabulated in TRS-398 (rev. 1) within the combined experimental uncertainty for the three residual ranges of 3.4, 13.3 and 27.7 g·cm-2. For Razor Nano chamber, k Q  values of 1.009 and 1.011 for residual ranges of 13.3 and 27.7 g·cm-2 have been determined. No recommended values are provided in TRS_398 (rev. 1). The overall budget yielded a combined standard uncertainty in the experimental k Q  determination of less than 1 %  ( k = 1  ). Conclusions: This study demonstrates the feasibility and high precision of using a portable graphite calorimeter for beam quality correction factor determination in the user beam quality. The short room occupation time required (around 3 hours) makes the system useful as well for beam output dosimetry audits without disturbing clinical practice.

items.title: Survival Outcomes With Lu-177 PSMA by Treatment Line and Taxane Sequencing in Prostate Cancer
items.authors: Nandakumar V, Jo Y, Ostrowski M, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Lutetium Lu 177 vipivotide tetraxetan (Lu-177) prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a targeted radioligand therapy approved for patients with metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant (mAPMR) prostate cancer after progression on androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs). Data to guide treatment sequencing are limited. Objective: To evaluate survival outcomes in patients with mAPMR prostate cancer receiving Lu-177 PSMA by line of therapy and the timing of taxane exposure. Design, Setting, And Participants: This cohort study used a deidentified electronic health record research database to obtain comprehensive longitudinal oncology data from community and academic practices across the US. Among patients with metastatic prostate cancer in the dataset, those who received Lu-177 PSMA after an ARPI between December 19, 2018, and June 23, 2025, met the inclusion criteria. The data cutoff was June 30, 2025. Exposure: Receipt of Lu-177 PSMA, stratified by line of therapy and timing of taxane exposure (before Lu-177 PSMA, after Lu-177 PSMA, or never received taxane). Main Outcomes And Measures: Primary end points were clinical time to next treatment (TTNT; defined as the time from Lu-177 PSMA initiation to next systemic therapy or death) and clinical overall survival (OS; defined as the time from Lu-177 PSMA initiation to death). Both outcomes were censored at last follow-up and estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method with 95% CIs. Results: Among the 850 patients included, the median (IQR) age was 74 (68-80) years; most were treated in community settings (598 [70.4%]) and had commercial insurance (520 [61.2%]). A total of 466 patients (54.8%) received taxane before Lu-177 PSMA, 35 (4.1%) received taxane after Lu-177 PSMA, and 349 (41.1%) never received taxane. Median clinical TTNT and clinical OS with Lu-177 PSMA were 8.0 (95% CI, 7.4-9.0) months and 12.0 (95% CI, 11.0-13.0) months for patients with taxane exposure before Lu-177 PSMA; 10.0 (95% CI, 9.2-11.0) months and 14.0 (95% CI, 13.0-17.0) months for patients who never received taxane; and 6.0 (95% CI, 4.9-8.0) months and 16.0 (95% CI, 13.0-not reached) months for patients with taxane exposure after Lu-177 PSMA, respectively. Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study, outcomes with Lu-177 PSMA were broadly consistent across treatment lines and taxane sequencing groups. These findings may help inform patient counseling, although prospective studies are needed to determine the optimal treatment sequencing strategy.

items.title: Digital and Coaching Interventions for Uptake of Cancer Genetic Testing: The MiGHT Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Austin S, Delacroix E, Rice JD, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Germline genetic testing (GT) for hereditary cancer risk can inform cancer treatment, screening, and prevention, yet testing rates remain low. Alternative strategies are needed to improve facilitation of GT. Objective: To compare 2 patient-level interventions to increase uptake of hereditary cancer GT against usual care. Design, Setting, And Participants: The Michigan Genetic Hereditary Testing (MiGHT) randomized clinical trial analyzed self-reported GT outcome data from participants meeting clinical GT criteria between April 21, 2022, and November 21, 2025. Participants were adults (age ≥18 years) who met national criteria for genetic evaluation and had not previously completed germline GT recruited from oncology, primary care, and gastroenterology practices; research registries; and the general public in Michigan. Data were analyzed from April 30, 2025, to May 1, 2026. Interventions: Participants were randomized to either telephone-based health coaching, a self-directed digital intervention, or usual care. Both interventions incorporated genetics education and motivational interviewing concepts. Main Outcomes And Measures: GT uptake was assessed at 6- and 12-month time points. The primary outcome was completion of GT by 6 months. The effects of study group on GT uptake were evaluated using logistic regression, adjusting for cancer history, age, gender, and race. Results: A total of 793 participants (median [IQR] age, 64 [51-71] years; 458 [57.8%] female) were randomized to health coaching (261 participants), the digital intervention (265 participants), or usual care (267 participants). Overall, 31 participants (4.9%) reported completing GT by the 6-month time point, and 76 participants (9.6%) underwent GT across the 12-month study period. Compared with usual care, participants in the digital intervention group had higher odds of completing GT by 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.88; 97.5% CI, 1.27-14.80), while those in the health coaching group had higher odds of completing GT by 12 months (AOR, 2.25; 97.5% CI, 1.11-4.77). Participants in the digital intervention group were more likely to express intention to test at 6 months (AOR, 2.36; 95% CI, 1.44-3.93), whereas those in the health coaching group had higher intention at both 6 (AOR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.83-4.95) and 12 (AOR, 2.29; 95% CI 1.29-4.15) months compared with usual care.…

items.title: Clinical Decision Support for Fall Prevention in Primary Care: The eSTEPS Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Latham NK, Hommel E, Kiesman M, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults. Although exercise reduces fall risk, implementation in primary care remains limited. Objective: To assess whether an electronic health record-integrated clinical decision support intervention, Electronic Strategies for Tailored Exercise to Prevent Falls (eSTEPS), reduces falls among older primary care patients at increased risk. Design, Setting, And Participants: This matched-pair cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted from June 9, 2023, to May 8, 2025, with 12 to 23 months of follow-up at primary care practices within an integrated health system in the US. Adults aged 65 years or older with a positive 3-item fall-risk screen at a primary care visit were included. Intervention: eSTEPS decision support embedded in the electronic health record with tailored exercise recommendations, optional physical therapy referral, and patient-facing materials (handouts, website, and app). Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was the rate of patients with 1 or more falls identified using electronic health record-derived International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) diagnostic codes. Secondary outcomes were the rate of patients with 1 or more fall-related injuries identified by validated ICD-10 algorithms and mortality. Results: Among 11 945 participants (mean [SD] age, 77.05 [7.43] years; 8044 females [67.3%]), of whom 5681 (47.6%) were in the intervention group and 6264 (52.4%) were in the control group, at 22 primary care practices, the rate of 1 or more ICD-10-coded falls (including falls with injuries) per 100 patient-years over the study period was 19.3 (95% CI, 18.6-20.1) in patients from intervention practices vs 21.2 (95% CI, 20.2-22.1) in patients from control practices (rate ratio [RR], 0.91 [95% CI, 0.88-0.95]; P < .001). The rate of ICD-10-coded fall-related injuries per 100 patient-years was 15.7 (95% CI, 15.0-16.5) from intervention practices vs 16.7 (95% CI, 16.1-17.4) from control practices over the study period (RR for fall injuries per 100 patient-years, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.90-0.97]; P = .001). No differences were observed in mortality. For intervention patients, eSTEPS exercise prescriptions were issued for 1255 patients (22.1%). Overall, 215 clinicians (77.9%) in intervention practices used the clinical decision support to deliver the exercise program at least once over the study period.…

items.title: Delayed elective nodal irradiation in head-and-neck cancer radiotherapy reduces acute lymphocyte damage, lymphopenia, and modulates immune signatures
items.authors: Kaufmann J, Salah A, Marini F, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Elective nodal irradiation (ENI) for locally advanced head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-HNSCC) contributes to hematotoxicity and may impair radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy. We investigated whether delayed ENI, using an upfront boost to gross disease and involved nodes followed by standard ENI, reduces radiation-induced lymphocyte DNA damage and lymphopenia (RIL) while modulating peripheral immune signaling compared with standard ENI. Materials And Methods: Twenty-eight LA-HNSCC patients assigned for adjuvant (n = 13) or definitive (n = 15) (chemo)radiotherapy were randomized to standard or delayed ENI (upfront boost: adjuvant: 2 × 2 Gy, n = 6/15; definitive: 5 × 2 Gy, n = 7/13). Blood was collected pre-treatment, 15 min and 24 h after the first fraction, and (definitive only) before fraction six and at treatment end. Primary endpoints: DNA damage in lymphocytes via γH2AX and 53BP1 foci (n = 25, pre-therapy, post-first and pre-sixth fraction) and dicentric chromosomes (n = 9, pre-therapy and pre-sixth fraction). Secondary endpoints: exploratory leukocyte transcriptomics (n = 4; pre-therapy, pre-sixth fraction and end of therapy), lymphocyte counts, and RIL (n = 28; pre-therapy and weekly during therapy). Results: Delayed ENI reduced initial planning target volume and whole-body dose by 9.9- and 4.4-fold (both p < 0.001), resulting in 3-4-fold lower DNA damage marker frequencies (p < 0.001) and fewer radiation-damaged lymphocytes (~11% vs. ~23%, p < 0.001). Baseline lymphocyte counts were preserved during the first treatment week, delaying RIL onset, whereas standard ENI induced an immediate decline in lymphocyte counts and RIL. Week 1 lymphocyte counts inversely correlated with planning target volume, whole-body dose, and DNA damage (all p < 0.01). Exploratory transcriptomic profiling revealed enhanced interferon and metabolic signaling with delayed ENI, whereas standard ENI preferentially activated inflammatory and damage-associated pathways. Conclusion: These findings suggest that delaying elective nodal irradiation may help preserve circulating immune cells during radiotherapy and provide a mechanistic rationale for future prospective studies evaluating whether this strategy can enhance radiotherapy-immunotherapy synergy in LA-HNSCC.
