items.title: A randomized, placebo-controlled, phase II study of docetaxel and platinum with or without erlotinib in recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas
items.authors: William WN Jr, Feng L, Kies MS, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. Patients And Methods: This was a placebo-controlled, double-blind, single-center phase II study. Patients (N = 120) were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive platinum (carboplatin area under the curve 6 or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) plus docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) with either erlotinib (150 mg/day orally until progression) or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, response rates, duration of response, and correlations of erlotinib-induced rash/biomarkers with outcomes. Results: Median PFS was 6.1 months with erlotinib versus 4.4 months with placebo [hazard ratio (HR) 0.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42-0.95, P = 0.026]. Median overall survival was 17.0 months in the erlotinib arm compared with 13.7 months in the control arm (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, P = 0.0718), meeting the prespecified type I error threshold. Subgroup analyses demonstrated numerically favorable PFS HRs across most clinical subgroups, with a more pronounced benefit observed in patients with oropharyngeal and human papillomavirus-related tumors. Development of grade ≥2 rash during the first cycle of erlotinib was associated with significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.87, P = 0.021). The addition of erlotinib increased the incidence of grade 2-4 adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal toxicity, rash, fatigue, and dehydration but no unexpected safety signals were observed. Conclusions: The study met its primary endpoint, supporting the continued relevance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibition in this disease. Although contemporary immunotherapy-based standards limit direct adoption of this regimen, these results provide clinically meaningful insight into EGFR biology and support further development of modernized, tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based EGFR strategies, including rational combinations and biomarker-driven approaches, to improve outcomes.

items.title: Associations between breast cancer and rheumatoid arthritis among older-age women in the United States
items.authors: Ahmed S, Seror R, Mariette X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Several studies have described an inverse association between rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and risk of breast cancer (BC), and one study reported lower risk of RA after BC. Factors contributing to this possibly bidirectional relationship remain unclear. Methods: Using the SEER-Medicare database (2008-2021), we conducted a case-control study to evaluate the association between RA and BC risk among women aged 66-99. RA was identified from Medicare claims. We also conducted a cohort study among BC cases and controls to evaluate subsequent RA incidence. Multivariable adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using generalized linear mixed models and hazard ratios (HRs) using Cox regression. Results: We included 204,186 BC cases and 2,897,862 controls. RA was inversely associated with BC (OR 0.80, 95%CI 0.77-0.83)-specifically, for hormone receptor positive BC (0.78, 0.76-0.81). In the cohort analysis (184,524 women with and without BC), BC was associated with lower incidence of RA (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.88-0.98). This association did not differ by BC hormone receptor status. Instead, among women with BC, radiotherapy was associated with reduced RA incidence (HR 0.82, 95%CI 0.76-0.89). Finally, among women with hormone receptor positive BC, treatment with exemestane was associated with increased incidence of RA (HR 1.33, 95%CI 1.17-1.50). Conclusion: These findings support a bidirectional inverse association between RA and BC. Hormone-related pathways may contribute to reduced BC risk in women with RA, whereas radiotherapy-related immune modulation may partly explain the lower incidence of RA incidence following BC. Further mechanistic studies are warranted.

items.title: Dose-Escalated Focal Salvage High-Dose-Rate Brachytherapy and Genomic Classifier Risk Stratification in Radiorecurrent Prostate Cancer: The F-SHARP Phase I/II Clinical Trial
items.authors: Solanki AA, Adams W, Proudfoot JA, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Prospective data on the management of intraprostatic radiorecurrence (IPR) after definitive radiotherapy (RT) and use of genomic classifiers (GC) in this setting are limited. We hypothesized that dose-escalated focal salvage high-dose-rate brachytherapy (DE-fsHDR) would be safe and effective, and that GC would risk stratify patients who may benefit from treatment intensification. Methods: F-SHARP is a multi-institutional phase I/II trial of DE-fsHDR for IPR after any form of RT for localized prostate cancer. Patients received up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions. The primary objective was to determine the acute RT-related grade ≥3 CTCAE v4.03 genitourinary and GI toxicity rates. Secondary end points included all-grade toxicity, quality of life (QoL; EPIC-26 and International Prostate Symptom Score), disease control, and survival. GC analysis used a clinical-grade transcriptome assay (Veracyte, San Diego, CA). Time-to-event outcomes included biochemical progression-free survival (bPFS), radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), local recurrence-free survival (LRFS), and metastasis-free survival (MFS). Results: Twenty-four participants received one fraction and 38 received two fractions (N = 62). The median follow-up was 39.4 months. No acute grade 3 toxicities occurred. Two patients (3.2%) had late grade 3 toxicity. QoL changes did not meet criteria for a minimal clinically important difference. Three-year survival rates were 62.7% (bPFS), 67.5% (rPFS), 73.0% (LRFS), and 85.9% (MFS); there were no differences between fractionation groups (all P > .05). Among 31 patients with GC results, higher scores were associated with worse bPFS, rPFS, LRFS, and MFS. All patients with GC score >0.85 (n = 4) experienced biochemical, local, and metastatic recurrence. Conclusion: DE-fsHDR is a safe and effective salvage treatment for IPR. GC score is a promising prognostic tool in patients undergoing salvage local therapy for IPR and warrants further study to guide treatment intensification.

items.title: Repeated metastasis-directed radiotherapy in patients with oligorecurrent prostate cancer: outcomes and risk stratification from a large multinational PSMA PET-guided cohort
items.authors: van der Walle R, van Bergen TD, Miszczyk M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Repeated metastasis-directed radiotherapy (MDRT) is increasingly used in patients with metachronous oligometastatic prostate cancer. However, the efficacy and optimal patient selection criteria remain insufficiently defined. Material And Methods: Within the multinational PORTAL consortium, we evaluated outcomes of repeated MDRT in patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET)-detected oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer undergoing ≥ 2 MDRT cycles. The primary endpoint was androgen deprivation therapy-free survival (ADT-FS), secondary endpoints included polymetastatic-free survival, next-line systemic therapy-free survival, and overall survival, all calculated from start of second MDRT. A multivariable Cox regression model was developed to predict ADT-FS, and its performance was evaluated by bootstrapped internal validation using discrimination (C-index) and calibration. Results: A total of 177 patients were included. Median follow-up after second MDRT was 26.1 months. During follow-up, 86 patients initiated ADT, 59 developed polymetastatic disease, 38 received next-line systemic therapy, and 17 deaths occurred. Two-year ADT-FS was 50.2 % (95 % CI 41.4-58.3). Two-year polymetastatic-free, next-line systemic therapy-free, and overall survival were 64.4 % (95 % CI 55.4-72.0), 83.5 % (95 % CI 76.0-88.9), and 94.2 % (95 % CI 88.2-97.2), respectively. In the multivariable Cox regression model, a longer interval between first and second MDRT (HR 0.96 per month, 95 % CI 0.94-0.99; p = 0.003) and treatment of a single versus ≥ 2 new lesions (HR for ≥ 2 lesions 1.88, 95 % CI 1.22-2.90; p = 0.006) were independently associated with ADT-FS. Model discrimination was moderate (optimism-corrected C-index 0.68) with good calibration. Conclusions: In this multicentre cohort of patients with PSMA PET-detected metachronous oligorecurrent prostate cancer undergoing repeated MDRT, favourable ADT-FS outcomes were observed, with approximately half of patients remaining ADT-free two years after second MDRT. Given the absence of a comparator group, these outcomes may reflect both the effects of treatment and favourable disease biology of patients who remained eligible for repeated MDRT. The interval between MDRT cycles, and the number of metastases, independently predicted ADT-FS and may support patient selection.

items.title: Multi-center comparison of relative stopping power estimation of an ex vivo phantom using clinical X-ray CT scanners and a proton CT prototype
items.authors: Fogazzi E, Bär E, Bruzzi M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Accurate estimation of relative stopping power (RSP) is essential for proton therapy (PT) treatment planning. Emerging X-ray computed tomography (xCT) technologies are enabling more advanced RSP calibration strategies, but may also introduce greater variability across centers. This study aimed to assess inter-center variability in xCT calibration and RSP estimation for proton treatment planning, using a proton CT (pCT) prototype as reference. Material And Methods: An ex vivo phantom was transported to five European PT centers and one research center, and scanned with both single-energy and dual-energy xCT systems. Acquisitions were performed in three phantom configurations, simulating different anatomical sizes. The reconstructed xCT images were calibrated to RSP according to each center's clinical protocol and compared against the pCT-derived RSP maps. Results: Voxel-by-voxel comparison between xCT-based and pCT-based RSP maps showed inter-center RSP variability of about 1% in soft tissues and up to 5% in bone, with larger differences observed for larger phantom sizes. The largest discrepancies (up to 5%) relative to pCT were observed in the same configurations. Centers implementing beam-hardening corrections generally showed closer agreement with pCT, whereas the effect of size-specific HLUTs was tissue- and anatomy-dependent. The impact of these RSP variations on water-equivalent thickness in representative clinical scenarios resulted in a 2σ inter-center variability of 1.09% and 1.39% for brain and prostate cases, respectively. Conclusions: This work presents the first inter-center comparison of xCT-based RSP estimation using an ex vivo phantom and pCT measurements as reference. The observed variability highlights the relevance of a comprehensive and standardized validation of xCT calibration protocols.

items.title: Combined pharmacologic and lifestyle intervention for breast cancer prevention: Results of the randomized phase II TOLERANT trial in high-risk women
items.authors: Serrano D, Lazzeroni M, Rizzo R, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Breast cancer (BC) prevention strategies include lifestyle modification and preventive agents such as selective estrogen receptor modulators and aromatase inhibitors. Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is a breast cancer risk-associated biomarker; however, it is not a validated surrogate endpoint for breast cancer risk reduction. Methods: Population: women with hereditary BC risk, a ≥ 5% 10-year BC risk, or a history of intraepithelial neoplasia were enrolled. Trial Design: a four-arm randomized phase II biomarker trial: Tamoxifen 10 mg every other day (LDT); LDT + Intermittent Caloric Restriction (ICR); Lifestyle intervention with a step counter (LI); LI + ICR. Primary Endpoint: Post intervention levels of circulating SHBG. Secondary endpoints: modulation of IGF system, adipokines, inflammatory markers, quality of life. Main analysis was LDT+ ICR vs LI+ICR. Results: One hundred and ten participants were randomized to: LDT, LDT plus ICR, LI, or LI plus ICR, for 6 months. Mean age was 52 years and mean BMI was 25 kg/m²; 62% were unaffected carriers, and 65% were postmenopausal. LDT±ICR significantly increased SHBG and IGFBP-3 and decreased IGF-I (absolute change p < 0.0001, p = 0.004, and p < 0.001, respectively). ICR arms showed higher adiponectin than non-ICR arms (p = 0.003). Furthermore, in adherent subjects (>90%), LI plus ICR was significantly associated with higher SHBG compared with LI alone (p = 0.045). No differences in adverse events between arms; LDT demonstrated a mild, although significant, worsening in quality of life. Conclusions: LDT favorably modulates BC risk-associated biomarkers, and ICR adds a complementary metabolic effect, supporting further investigation of these combined strategies.

items.title: Effects of adjunctive metformin on recurrence-free survival and reproductive outcomes following progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment for endometrial neoplasia: Results from the FELICIA trial, a prospective, randomized, phase IIb trial with blinded central adjudication
items.authors: Mitsuhashi A, Yamagami W, Inaba Y, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Metformin is a potential anticancer agent; however, evidence of benefit in endometrial neoplasia is limited. We evaluated whether adding metformin improved the outcomes of progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment. Methods: In this multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase IIb trial using blinded central adjudication, women aged 18-42years with an institutional diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) or presumed stage IA grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma were assigned (1:1:1) to medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) alone, MPA plus metformin 750mg/day, or MPA plus metformin 1500mg/day. Central pathological review reclassified baseline specimens according to the 2020 World Health Organization criteria and adjudicated remission and recurrence. The primary endpoint was the 3-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate from treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included remission, pregnancy outcomes, and safety. Results: Analysis included 154 patients. Median body mass index was 24.3 (range, 15.6-57.1) kg/m2. The Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 3-year RFS rate were 44.7% with MPA alone and 44.5% with the pooled metformin groups. The prespecified log-rank test showed no significant difference (P=0.825). Remission rates were 54.0%, 58.8%, and 50.9% in the MPA-alone, metformin 750mg, and metformin 1500mg groups, respectively. Among the 57 women who attempted to conceive, pregnancy occurred in 36.8%, 57.9%, and 42.1%, and live birth in 31.6%, 52.6%, and 31.6%, respectively. Metformin increased gastrointestinal adverse events and was associated with less MPA-associated weight gain; no new safety signals emerged. Conclusion: Adding metformin to MPA did not improve RFS or remission rates, suggesting limited benefit in fertility-sparing treatment of endometrial neoplasia.

items.title: Patient selection for proton therapy in lung cancer: Updating and internal-external cross-validation of a normal tissue complication probability model for acute oesophageal toxicity
items.authors: Wijsman R, van Loon JGM, Bartels R, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To externally validate and update a published normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) model for the prediction of Grade ≥ 2 acute oesophageal toxicity (AOT) in lung cancer patients receiving (chemo-)radiotherapy (predictors: concurrent chemotherapy, gender, tumour stage, mean oesophagus dose (MOD)). Methods And Materials: Patient cohorts from four centres were available. Initial external validation was performed by assessing model performance. Heterogeneity of performance across cohorts was evaluated using an internal-external cross validation (IECV) method. Based on the IECV procedure, parameters were added or removed from the model to lower heterogeneity in model performance across cohorts with the aim to create a model that performed uniformly well across centres. Ridge regression was used to create the final model and bootstrapping techniques were applied to perform further internal validation. Results: Out of 937 patients, 444 (47%) had Grade ≥ 2 AOT. External validation indicated model recalibration was necessary for 1 cohort and model revision for another. IECV showed heterogeneity of performance of the original model across cohorts. To lower heterogeneity in model performance, the predictors concurrent chemotherapy, gender, and tumour stage were removed from the model, and overall treatment time (OTT) was added. The final model containing MOD and OTT as predictors showed low levels of heterogeneity in model performance (I2 of 0% for all performance measures) with optimism-corrected AUC of 0.75, calibration intercept of -0.01 and slope of 1.26. Conclusion: The validation and updating of an NTCP-model for AOT resulted in a prediction model performing well in varying patient cohorts. Therefore, this updated model was added to the national indication protocol to select lung cancer patients for proton radiotherapy.

items.title: Ponatinib-Blinatumomab or Imatinib-Chemotherapy for Adult Ph-Positive ALL
items.authors: Chiaretti S, Piciocchi A, Skert C, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The outcome of Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-positive ALL) has greatly improved with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy. Methods: In this trial, we randomly assigned adult patients with Ph-positive ALL in a 2:1 ratio to receive ponatinib plus blinatumomab (intervention group) or imatinib plus chemotherapy (control group) as frontline treatment. A crossover to the intervention group was allowed for patients with persistence or reappearance of measurable residual disease in the control group. The primary end point was event-free survival. Results: A total of 236 patients underwent randomization: 158 to the intervention group and 78 to the control group. The median age of the patients was 55 years (range, 24 to 82). At a median follow-up of 23.7 months, the estimated 24-month event-free survival was 86% in the intervention group and 67% in the control group (P<0.001). Survival with no measurable residual disease was 68% and 42%, respectively. At the end of induction, a complete hematologic response was observed in 94% of the patients in the intervention group and in 79% of those in the control group. After blinatumomab consolidation, a molecular response was observed in 71% and 49% of the patients, respectively. After crossover to the intervention group, 20 of 31 patients (64%) had a molecular response. Overall survival was 90% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group. The cumulative incidence of relapse was 5% and 13%, respectively. As of this report, only 19% of the patients in the intervention group had undergone hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation after having had a first complete hematologic response. Conclusions: In this phase 3 trial, a frontline chemotherapy-free targeted and immunotherapeutic approach was superior to the use of imatinib and chemotherapy. (Funded by Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro and others; GIMEMA ALL2820 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04722848.).

items.title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
items.authors: Lebow ES, Shih HA
items.abstract: Abstract Proton therapy offers a distinct physical advantage over photon radiotherapy through the Bragg peak dose concentration in target with both lower integral dose and finite path length, and sharper penumbra as compared to photons, collectively reducing radiation exposure to surrounding normal tissues and potentially improving the therapeutic ratio. However, this advantage is tempered by uncertainties, including range uncertainty and variable relative biological effectiveness. In this review, the authors summarize contemporary evidence supporting proton therapy across pediatric, central nervous system (CNS), head and neck, thoracic, breast, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and hematologic malignancies, as well as reirradiation. The strength of evidence varies substantially by disease site. Proton therapy is well established in pediatric cancers and selected CNS tumors, where minimizing integral dose and late toxicity is especially important. Randomized trials have demonstrated clinically meaningful benefits in selected settings, including improved disease control and survival with proton craniospinal irradiation for leptomeningeal metastases and reduced toxicity with preserved disease control and survival benefit in oropharyngeal cancer. Conversely, randomized data in localized prostate cancer have not shown improved patient reported outcomes compared with intensity modulated photon therapy. Ongoing phase 3 trials across multiple disease sites are expected to further define the role of protons by clarifying comparative effectiveness, toxicity reduction, and cost‐effectiveness relative to advanced photon techniques. Future progress will depend on improved patient selection, robust treatment planning, and emerging technologies including adaptive proton therapy, proton arc therapy, and FLASH radiotherapy.

items.title: Association between Trust and Patient-Reported Outcomes and Experience in Prostate Cancer Patients
items.authors: Chhatre S, Gallo JJ, Guzzo T, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the association between patient-physician trust, treatment choice, patient-reported outcomes, and patient-reported experiences among patients with localized prostate cancer. Materials And Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of data from a multicenter randomized controlled trial among patients with localized prostate cancer. Trust was measured at baseline, prior to treatment, using the Patient Trust-Wake Forest Physician Trust Scale (PTWF). Outcomes were assessed at baseline and at 3, 6, 12, and 24 mo. Treatments were robotic-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy, radiation therapy, and active surveillance. The primary treatment outcome was receipt of active treatment (surgery or radiation therapy) versus active surveillance. Multivariable logistic regression and linear mixed-effects models were adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, marital status, education, employment, insurance, prostate cancer risk group, intervention assignment, and study site. Sensitivity analyses modeling trust as a continuous variable yielded findings that were materially consistent with the primary analyses. Results: The high-trust group had higher odds of receiving active treatment than the low-trust group did (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.14-2.87; P = 0.013). Higher baseline trust was also consistently associated with better physical and mental health-related quality of life and higher satisfaction with care and treatment decision making across follow-up assessments through 24 mo. Sensitivity analyses using trust as a continuous measure produced similar findings. Conclusions: Higher patient-physician trust was independently associated with treatment choice, patient-reported outcomes, and patient-reported experience. These findings underscore the importance of patient-physician trust as a component of patient-centered cancer care and shared decision making. Future studies should evaluate interventions designed to strengthen trust and improve patient-centered outcomes across diverse clinical settings.

items.title: Prostate Cancer Incidence and Disease Characteristics in Transgender Women Receiving Gender-affirming Hormone Therapy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
items.authors: Oberoi K, Trevaskis I, Hassan S, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Objective: Transgender women (TGW) retain lifelong prostate cancer (PCa) risk despite gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT), yet its association with PCa incidence and severity is poorly synthesised. This study aimed to quantify pooled PCa incidence in TGW on GAHT relative to cisgender men and characterise disease severity. Methods: This is a systematic review with meta-analysis per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews: CRD420261369142). Five databases were searched from inception to April 2026. Eligible studies reported PCa incidence or outcomes in ≥5 TGW or gender-diverse individuals with intact prostates receiving GAHT. Screening, extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions; JBI) were performed in duplicate. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled standardised incidence ratios (SIR), incidence rates, and proportions with recorded PCa. Key Findings And Limitations: Nine studies drawn from six independent data sources (54 342 TGW on GAHT; 160 PCa cases) were included. Pooled SIR versus age-adjusted cisgender men was 0.224 (95% confidence interval = 0.146-0.344; κ = 2), a 77.6% relative reduction; pooled incidence rate was 22.9 versus 98.1 per 100 000 person-years. Among 36 cases with reported grade, 33.3% were International Society of Urological Pathology grade group 4-5; prostate-specific antigen (PSA) ranged from 6.5-18.0 ng/ml and was not pooled. Grade and stage data were derived from fewer than 40 patients with no matched cisgender comparison. Conclusions And Clinical Implications: Detected PCa incidence is substantially lower in TGW receiving GAHT, on very low certainty evidence. Case-level data include a non-negligible proportion of high-grade disease, but whether severity differs from matched cisgender populations remains uncertain. Clinicians should not equate population-level reduction with individual-level protection. Validated PSA thresholds and screening pathways are needed.

items.title: Radiotherapy combined with serplulimab, and chemotherapy as first-line treatment for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma: a multicenter, single-arm, phase II trial
items.authors: Cheng K, Zhang C, Liu J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The prognosis for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) remains dismal. In this multicenter, single-arm, phase II study, we evaluated the combination of serplulimab, gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, and radiotherapy (ICSBR regimen) as first-line treatment for mPDAC patients (ChiCTR2300073237). Methods: Patients with mPDAC were enrolled in the first-line setting. The treatment regimen consisted of serplulimab and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel administered in 21-day cycles, combined with stereotactic body radiotherapy directed at the primary or metastatic sites during cycle 2. Additionally, comprehensive biomarker analysis was conducted. The primary endpoint was the 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate, with a predefined target of 60%. Result: Forty-six patients received at least one dose of treatment. The 6-month PFS rate was 78.3% (95% CI, 67.2%-91.1%). The median PFS and overall survival (OS) were 8.5 months (95% CI, 7.3-12.0 months) and 14.0 months (95% CI, 12.0 months-not reached), respectively. The objective response rate was 73.9% (95% CI, 58.9%-85.7%). The combination treatment was well tolerated, and no treatment-related deaths or unexpected safety signals were observed. Notably, patients with baseline ctDNA negativity achieved a better survival. Moreover, tumor microenvironment (TME) analysis revealed that baseline fibroblast activation protein-positive cancer-associated fibroblast and T-cell proportions in tumor tissue correlated with clinical outcomes, with distinct spatial distribution and interaction tendencies observed among patients with different responses. Conclusion: Overall, the ICSBR regimen demonstrated a promising survival benefit as first-line treatment for mPDAC. Furthermore, ctDNA status and TME analysis highlighted potential markers for guiding precision treatment.

items.title: Pan-Asian adapted ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with early and locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer
items.authors: Hayashi H, Zer A, Kenmotsu H, et al.
items.abstract: The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with early and locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) were published in August 2025 and were adapted in November 2025 according to previously established standard methodology to produce the Pan-Asian adapted ESMO consensus guidelines for the management of Asian patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC. The adapted guidelines presented in this article represent the consensus opinions reached by a panel of Asian experts on the treatment of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC representing the oncological societies of China (Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology), Indonesia (Indonesian Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology), India (Indian Society of Medical and Paediatric Oncology), Japan [Japanese Society of Medical Oncology (JSMO)], South Korea (Korean Society of Medical Oncology), Malaysia (Malaysian Oncological Society), the Philippines (Philippine Society of Medical Oncology), Singapore (Singapore Society of Oncology), Taiwan (Taiwan Oncology Society) and Thailand (Thai Society of Clinical Oncology), coordinated by ESMO and JSMO. The voting was based on scientific evidence and was independent of the current treatment practices, drug access restrictions and reimbursement decisions in the different regions of Asia. The latter are discussed separately in the article. The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in the drug approvals and reimbursement strategies among the different regions.

items.title: Adverse events in gynaecological radiotherapy: Better Reporting, Interpretation and Dissemination to Generate Evidence (BRIDGE)
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Spampinato S, Burchardt E, Stankiewicz M, et al.
items.abstract: Accurate adverse events (AE) reporting is essential in gynaecological radiotherapy, as multimodal approaches become increasingly common. While these strategies improve outcomes, they may increase the risk of complications affecting patients' quality of life. The BRIDGE (Better Reporting, Interpretation and Dissemination to Generate Evidence) initiative aims to improve consistency and understanding in AE assessment across the radiotherapy community. This analysis investigated whether interpretation of the same clinical information leads to variability in AE grading using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v6.0. An interactive poll conducted during an ESTRO webinar used two clinical scenarios. Among 71 attendees, 30 responded to the poll and 23 consented to share their data. Variation in severity scoring was observed, especially for subjective and lower-grade AEs, whereas higher agreement occurred when clinical details aligned with CTCAE terminology. Findings highlight the importance of training, clear clinical context, and integration of patient-reported outcomes to support person-centred care.

items.title: Effects of rectal retractor use on dosimetric parameters, treatment-related adverse events, and clinical outcomes of cervical cancer brachytherapy: A retrospective tertiary-centre study
items.authors: Hazırbulan A, Kızıltan HŞ, Çepni K, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: We assessed whether rectal retractor use was associated with dose parameters, organ volumes, treatment-related adverse events, and oncological outcomes in patients who underwent cervical cancer brachytherapy. Materials And Methods: This retrospective study included 148 patients treated with intracavitary brachytherapy between June 2020 and June 2025. Patients treated with and without a rectal retractor were compared regarding dosimetric, volumetric, adverse event, and survival outcomes. Adverse events were graded via RTOG criteria. Cumulative dose parameters were calculated using EQD2. ROC analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed to evaluate factors associated with grade ≥ 2 adverse events. Results: Rectal retractor use occurred in 58 patients (39.2%). Baseline demographic characteristics and tumour size were comparable between groups, although rectal retractor use differed according to applicator type. Rectal retractor use was associated with lower rectal D2cc (no retractor vs. retractor: 65.70 Gy vs. 60.79 Gy, p = 0.002) but higher bladder D2cc (no retractor vs. retractor: 75.59 Gy vs. 80.08 Gy, p < 0.001) values. Prescribed EQD2, HR-CTV coverage, sigmoid D2cc, and volumetric parameters were similar. Grade ≥ 2 vaginal adverse events were less frequent in the retractor group than in the no-retractor group (32.8% vs. 56.7%, p = 0.004). No significant difference was observed in grade ≥ 2 rectal (p = 0.380) or urinary adverse events (p = 0.083). ROC analysis showed that first-fraction volumetric parameters had limited discriminatory ability for grade ≥ 2 adverse events (AUC range: 0.417-0.613). In multivariable analysis, rectal retractor use was associated with lower odds of grade ≥ 2 vaginal adverse events (OR 0.29; 95% CI, 0.13-0.63; p = 0.002). Conclusions: Rectal retractor use was associated with rectal dose sparing and lower odds of grade ≥ 2 vaginal adverse events without compromising target coverage. However, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because rectal retractor placement was not randomised and was influenced by applicator compatibility.

items.title: Laser Therapy for Sexual Health in Breast Cancer Survivors Receiving Aromatase Inhibitors: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Anglès-Acedo S, Alonso I, Ribera-Torres L, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Laser therapy is increasingly used to treat genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) in breast cancer survivors, but sham-controlled evidence of benefit remains limited. Objective: To evaluate 12-month efficacy and safety of fractional carbon dioxide (CO2) laser therapy (CLT) vs sham laser therapy (SLT) for GSM in breast cancer survivors receiving aromatase inhibitors. Design, Setting, And Participants: This is a secondary analysis of a single-center, double-blind, sham-controlled randomized clinical trial conducted at a tertiary academic hospital in Spain. Participants included breast cancer survivors with GSM and dyspareunia receiving aromatase inhibitors, recruited from October 30, 2020, to September 1, 2021. Participants were followed up for 12 months. Data were analyzed from December 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025. Intervention: Five monthly sessions of CLT or SLT plus first-line nonhormonal therapy (FLT), including vaginal moisturizers and vibrators. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) score. Secondary outcomes included rate of sexual activity, dyspareunia, Spanish Body Image Scale, quality of life (12-Item Short Form Health Survey), Vaginal Health Index, objective parameters (pH, vaginal maturation index, epithelial measures), serum estradiol level, FLT adherence, and adverse events. Results: Of the 84 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 53.8 [8.8] years), 67 completed the 12-month follow-up (CLT, 32; SLT, 35). The CLT group did not differ from the SLT group in FSFI score change from baseline to 12 months (difference, CLT vs SLT, -0.69 [95% CI, -3.58 to 2.20]; P = .64), nor in any secondary outcome. Across the full sample, significant improvements from baseline to 12 months were observed in FSFI score (18.9 to 23.0; mean difference, 4.5 [95% CI, 3.1-5.9]; P < .001), dyspareunia (mean difference, -3.7 [95% CI, -4.4 to -3.0]; P < .001), Spanish Body Image Scale (mean difference, -3.9 [95% CI, -5.1 to -2.8]; P < .001), and Vaginal Health Index (mean difference, 4.2 [95% CI, 3.1-5.2]; P < .001). Sexual activity increased among 57 of 67 participants (85.1%; odds ratio, 2.35 [95% CI, 1.23-4.50]; P = .009). Improvements were found in pH (mean difference, -0.5 [95% CI, -0.8 to -0.2]; P < .001) and vaginal maturation index (mean difference, 19.0% [95% CI, 13.4%-24.5%]; P < .001). FLT adherence was similar between groups. No severe adverse effects occurred.…

items.title: A Clinical Dose Prescription System for Proton Radiotherapy Based on the Mayo Clinic Florida Microdosimetric Kinetic Model
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Parisi A, Furutani KM, Hartzell S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Clinical proton dose prescription uses a fixed relative biological effectiveness (RBE) factor of 1.1 despite preclinical and clinical evidence that RBE varies with dose, radiation quality, and tissue radiosensitivity, particularly near the distal edge of treatments. We present a proton clinical dose-prescription system which: (1) is consistent with the clinical RBE of 1.1 for target dose definition, (2) uses full microdosimetric spectral distributions including primary and secondary ions, and (3) accounts for RBE variations in a framework analogous to that clinically used in carbon ion radiotherapy. Methods And Materials: Monte Carlo simulations were performed using OpenTOPAS. The clinical dose was defined as the product of the absorbed dose, the biological RBE calculated with the Mayo Clinic Florida microdosimetric kinetic model (MCF MKM) relative to the mid of a reference 2 Gy (RBE) spread-out Bragg peak, and a clinical scaling factor. The clinical dose system was evaluated across various dose levels, target depths, and spread-out Bragg peak widths. The results were compared with calculations using the fixed RBE factor and two approaches based on the dose-averaged linear energy transfer of protons only (Beltran and McNamara models). Results: Across the investigated scenarios, the target-averaged MCF MKM-based RBE ranged from 1.08 to 1.18. The corresponding target-averaged RBE values obtained with the McNamara and the Beltran models were on average 1% lower (range, 86%-105%) and 9% higher (range, 103%-122%), respectively. For all models, substantially higher RBE values were observed at the distal edge and out-of-field. Conclusions: This work establishes a clinical dose system for proton radiotherapy inspired by the corresponding Japanese system for carbon ions. The proposed approach maintains consistency with historical proton practice based on a fixed RBE of 1.1 and accounts for the spatial variations of the radiation quality using microdosimetric distributions that include all primary and secondary ions.

items.title: Engaging With Medical Evidence in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Health care is, in part, an information science. Delivering optimal care requires clinicians to continually find, evaluate, and apply an expanding body of medical knowledge when caring for patients. Textbooks, journals, and expert-authored online resources have long helped clinicians navigate this task. However, practice is changing with the rapid growth and use of artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled platforms that offer seemingly more sophisticated assistance: searches tailored to key clinical details, interactive literature summaries with hyperlinks to the highest-ranked evidence sources, and tailored diagnostic and treatment recommendations. These advances extend beyond how information is retrieved to how clinicians learn, assess evidence, and determine its relevance to the patients they care for.

items.title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform
items.authors: Patel VR, Finlayson SG, Liu-Hass M, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited. Objective: To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries. Design, Setting, And Participants: This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries. Main Outcomes And Measures: The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined. Results: Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians. Conclusions And Relevance: Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.

items.title: Transoral robotic versus laser surgery for cT1-T3 supraglottic laryngeal cancers: a systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative and non-comparative studies
items.authors: Lechien JR, Vaira LA, Baudouin R, et al.
items.abstract: Background: To compare literature findings about functional, oncological and surgical outcomes of transoral robotic (TORS) versus transoral laser microsurgery (TOLM) for supraglottic cT1-T3 laryngeal cancers. Methods: Three independent investigators conducted a PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Library search for papers reporting oncological, functional and surgical (complications) outcomes of TOLM and TORS. Outcomes were statistically compared considering controlled (direct) studies, and indirectly between single-arm cohort studies. Results: Fifty studies (2,644 patients) were included: 19 single-arm TORS (n = 615), 27 single-arm TOLM (n = 1,122), and four comparative studies (n = 907). Pooled positive margins were 7.3% (95%CI, 4.3-12.0) after TORS and 12.7% (8.6-18.3) after TOLM (P = 0.08); the comparative meta-analysis yielded a risk ratio of 0.65 (0.21-1.99; P = 0.45), also favoring TORS non-significantly. No difference was found for postoperative hemorrhage (5.8% versus 6.4%; P = 0.79) or permanent gastrostomy (7.4% versus 4.8%; P = 0.33). Permanent tracheostomy was rare in both groups (1.6% versus 1.3%), and laryngeal preservation reached 99.6% and 93.0%, respectively. Complication rates were not poolable for TOLM (I2 = 87.0%) owing to definitional heterogeneity. Five-year overall survival was 72.6% (65.8-78.4) in the TOLM series and not poolable for TORS. Median follow-up was 26 versus 50 months. Conclusion: TORS and TOLM provide currently comparable oncological, surgical, and functional outcomes in cT1-T3 supraglottic LSCC. Direct and indirect evidence converged toward a non-significant margin advantage for TORS. Apparent differences across the literature more plausibly reflect case mix, era, follow-up duration, and outcome definitions than the surgical technique itself. Randomized comparisons in matched populations are critically needed.

items.title: Loncastuximab and Rituximab in Elderly Unfit/Frail Patients With Previously Untreated Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
items.authors: Nair R, Kumar A, Chapman AE, et al.
items.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) therapy is typically treated with multi-agent chemotherapy with curative intent but is often challenging or poorly tolerated in patients who are elderly, frail, or have significant comorbidities. LOTIS-9 was a phase 2 trial of loncastuximab tesirine (loncastuximab tesirine-lpyl [Lonca]) plus rituximab (Lonca-R) in patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL who were unfit (cohort A) or frail with or without cardiac comorbidities (cohort B), the majority of whom typically would be ineligible for trials. Patients received Lonca (150 µg/kg during cycles 1-2, 75 µg/kg for subsequent cycles) and R (375 mg/m2) intravenously Q3W for 3-6 cycles, adapted based on response after cycle 3. The primary endpoint of cohort A was complete response (CR) rate; coprimary endpoints of cohort B were CR rate and proportion of patients who completed treatment per protocol. The median age was 84 years (range, 80-91) in cohort A (n=17) and 80 years (range, 67-92) in cohort B (n=24). The CR rates were 52.9% (A: 9/17) and 41.7% (B: 10/24), respectively. In cohort B, 8 (33.3%) patients completed treatment. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 31 (75.6%) patients, including 11 fatal events. Due to toxicity concerns in this medically fragile population, LOTIS-9 was voluntarily terminated prematurely though meaningful efficacy was demonstrated in patients who typically would be ineligible for clinical trials and/or standard of care therapies. These findings provide important insights for future trials. Additional investigation of targeted therapies in vulnerable unfit and frail patients with DLBCL is warranted. (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05144009).

items.title: AI in Proton Therapy Treatment Planning: A Narrative Review
items.authors: Ding Y, Feng H, Bues M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Proton therapy provides superior dose conformity compared to photon therapy, but its treatment planning is challenged by sensitivity to anatomical changes, setup/range uncertainties, and computational complexity. This narrative review evaluates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving proton therapy treatment planning, with emphasis on proton-specific requirements for dose-calculation accuracy, robustness, and adaptive decision-making. Materials And Methods: Recent studies on AI applications across the proton therapy planning workflow, including imaging, registration, segmentation, contour assessment, dose prediction/denoising, optimization, adaptive therapy, and large language model (LLM) and multimodal AI were reviewed and summarized by application domain and validation strategy. Both proton-therapy-specific studies and selected general radiotherapy AI studies were included when they introduced methods relevant to proton treatment planning, with attention to the additional validation needed for proton therapy. Results: AI has shown promise in enhancing imaging for dose calculation, automating contouring and contour assessment, accelerating dose calculation, predicting and denoising dose distributions, supporting robust optimization, and improving adaptive planning workflows. Compared with photon therapy, AI tools in proton therapy require more stringent evaluation because errors in AI-generated images, deformation fields, contours, dose estimates, or optimization outputs may propagate into water-equivalent path length, range uncertainty, scenario-specific dose distributions, and adaptive replanning decisions. Emerging applications, including LLMs and multimodal foundation models, may further support clinical-context integration, treatment-planning documentation, plan review, and workflow coordination. Key limitations include data scarcity, limited generalizability, physical interpretability, uncertainty management, lack of standardized proton-specific benchmarks, and limited prospective validation. Conclusion: AI is emerging as a key enabler of efficient, consistent, and patient-specific proton therapy treatment planning. Clinical translation will require interpretable and physics-aware models, multi-institutional validation, workflow-level testing, and evaluation using proton-specific endpoints such as HU/RSP accuracy, range error, dose-calculation accuracy, robustness, deliverability, and adaptive decision consistency.

items.title: End-to-end automated radiotherapy planning using transfer learning to overcome data scarcity
items.authors: Jiang L, Hirata E, Porter E, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose To develop and benchmark 3D dose prediction algorithms for volumetric modulated arc therapy for head‐and‐neck (HN) and pancreatic cancer treatments, and to demonstrate the clinical feasibility of converting the predicted doses into deliverable plans. Methods and materials Three deep learning models were pretrained on 3232 public plans and fine‐tuned on institutional cohorts (256 HN and 72 pancreas patients). The accuracy of the fine‐tuning strategy was compared with the baseline trained from scratch using only institutional data. In a prospective setting, the predicted dose was used as the planning goal for fully automated plan generation. Automated plans were benchmarked against clinical plans using Plan Quality Metrics. The deliverability of the fully automated plans was verified by Mobius ion‐chamber patient‐specific quality assurance (PSQA). Results Relative to training from scratch, transfer learning significantly accelerated convergence and minimized prediction error in scenarios with limited site‐specific data. For HN cases, fine‐tuning yielded a prediction error of 1.76 Gy. Notably, models fine‐tuned on just 5% (n = 12) of the dataset achieved accuracy comparable to models trained from scratch using 50% (n = 116) of the training data. In the pancreas cohort, fine‐tuning resulted in a mean absolute error of 1.35 Gy, representing a 14.6% reduction compared to the baseline trained solely on institutional data. When used for automated planning, these predicted 3D doses improved planning target volume homogeneity and organs at risk sparing (esophagus and trachea) in HN plans, while pancreas plans aimed to meet clinical goals with reduced dose to the spinal cord and right kidney. All automated plans were confirmed as clinically deliverable via PSQA. Conclusion Compared with models trained from scratch on institutional data, transfer learning significantly reduced prediction error and improved robustness. The feasibility of converting predicted doses into clinical plans while maintaining plan quality through a fully automated process was demonstrated.

items.title: An in-house timer for ART-specific extra time in gynecologic pelvic online adaptive radiation therapy
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Zheng Y, Lei R, Qu A, et al.
items.abstract: Online adaptive radiation therapy (ART) lengthens the session, but many published times report one interval and do not isolate ART-specific activity. We developed a console timer that records wall-clock timestamps for a defined event list, stores per-fraction ART settings, and exports Excel tables. ART-specific extra time extends from ART mode until plan approval. After verification on 100 simulated fractions, it was applied in 38 fan-beam CT-guided gynecologic pelvic online ART fractions (nine patients). Mean ART-specific extra time was 13.7 min within a 21.8-min session, dominated by optimization and target/organ-at-risk editing. It supports bottleneck audit under a shared event list.

items.title: Comparative toxicity and efficacy of consolidative thoracic radiotherapy after first-line chemoimmunotherapy in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: real-world retrospective cohort study
items.authors: Bai B, Jiang Y, Meng H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: First-line chemoimmunotherapy (CT-IT) is the standard treatment for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC), while consolidative thoracic radiotherapy (cTRT) may improve local control and survival. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of cTRT after first-line CT-IT in patients with ES-SCLC in a real-world setting. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 199 patients with ES-SCLC who received first-line CT-IT. Patients were divided into a CT-IT + cTRT group (n = 97) and a CT-IT alone group (n = 102). Survival outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). Treatment-related adverse events were assessed. Results: The two groups were generally comparable at baseline, although the CT-IT + cTRT group had fewer brain metastases and more favorable response-related features after induction treatment. Median PFS and OS were significantly longer in the CT-IT + cTRT group (both P < 0.001). cTRT (P < 0.001) and a longer duration of maintenance immunotherapy (P = 0.031) were independently associated with a better PFS. For OS, cTRT was associated with better survival status (P = 0.003) and liver metastasis with poorer survival status (P = 0.015). Regarding safety, grade 1-2 dermatitis and gastrointestinal toxicity were more frequent in the CT-IT + cTRT group, whereas rates of pneumonitis, esophagitis, immune-related adverse events, and grade 3-4 toxicities were comparable between groups. Conclusion: In this real-world retrospective cohort, the addition of cTRT to first-line CT-IT was associated with significantly improved PFS and OS in patients with ES-SCLC, without an apparent increase in severe treatment-related toxicity. Prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings and refine patient selection for cTRT.

items.title: Communicating Uncertainties About the Benefits and Risks of New Cancer Drugs: Two Randomized Clinical Trials
items.authors: Cherla A, Wagner AK, Woloshin S, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Cancer drugs are frequently approved based on uncertain benefits and risks that are not communicated to patients. Objective: To evaluate the effect of communicating uncertainties about the benefits and risks of new cancer drugs on changes in individuals' hypothetical decisions to take the drug. Design, Setting, And Participants: Two randomized clinical trials recruited online a demographically diverse sample of US adults (census matched for age, sex, education, income, and race and ethnicity) from May 9 to July 26, 2025. Intervention: Plain-language statements describing uncertainties about drug benefits and risks. Trial 1 randomized participants to 1 of 5 uncertainties: (1) single-arm trial design, (2) unrepresentative population in terms of race and ethnicity, (3) short study duration, (4) surrogate end point, or (5) no noticeable improvement. Trial 2 randomized participants to 1, 2, 3, or 4 uncertainties or to a control group. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome in trial 1 was changes in hypothetical decisions to take a new cancer drug (within-group difference), while in trial 2 the primary outcome was the change in between-group differences in hypothetical decisions (control vs intervention groups). Secondary outcomes included perceived treatment effectiveness, worry associated with taking the drug, and trust in the information and the US Food and Drug Administration. Results: A total of 6272 adults were included in the primary analysis (3102 [49.5%] women). In trial 1, learning about uncertainties reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug by a mean of 10.1 percentage points (pp; 95% CI, -11.7 to -8.5 pp; P < .001). The reduction in hypothetical decisions to take the drug was observed for all uncertainties, including among those in the group that learned that it was unknown whether patients would notice an improvement with the drug (-14.1 pp; 95% CI, -17.9 to -10.4 pp; P < .001) and those who learned that the drug was not studied in patients of similar race or ethnicity (-12.8 pp; 95% CI, -16.4 to -9.2; P < .001). In trial 2, hypothetical decisions to take the drug decreased with each additional uncertainty, demonstrating a dose-dependent effect. Learning about uncertainties reduced perceived effectiveness and trust but did not affect worry. Conclusions And Relevance: In 2 randomized clinical trials including a demographically diverse sample of US adults, learning about common uncertainties with a new cancer drug's benefits and risks reduced hypothetical decisions to take the drug.…

items.title: Adoption and Practice Patterns of TG-263 Standardized Nomenclature for Breast Radiation Therapy in a Statewide Quality Consortium
items.authors: Moncion A, Bains J, Grubb M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To assess the compliance rates of a national nomenclature standard (TG-263) in a collaborative quality consortium to determine compliance trends over time and the impact of insurance-based incentive programs on adoption, common naming errors, and differences in compliance between teaching and non-teaching centers for breast radiation therapy. Materials/Methods: DICOM submissions were used to verify TG-263 compliance of breast treatment plan structures for the breast target volumes, surgical bed, heart, and ipsilateral lung. Annual compliance rates were analyzed using the Cochran-Armitage test, and rates were summarized across 29 participating centers and compared between teaching and non-teaching centers. Results: TG-263 naming practice patterns were analyzed for 12,853 patients receiving breast radiation therapy at teaching and non-teaching centers between 2018 and 2024. The PTV_Breast_L/R compliance improved from 85.2% to 97.1% from 2018 to 2024. PTVsb compliance increased from 86.5% to 90.9% from 2018 to 2024. In 2024, a difference in compliance was only observed for PTV_Breast_L/R, with rates of 91.1% and 97.7% for teaching and non-teaching centers, respectively. Compliance with naming both PTV_Breast_L/R and PTVsb correctly was 77.2% in 2018 and 89.4% in 2024. The most common non-compliant structure name that was submitted was 'PTV_Boost_L/R'. Conclusion: This study shows that initiatives can be used to improve TG-263 compliance and thus enhance terminology adoption and inter- and intra- clinical communication, which is maintained after the incentives end.

items.title: Selpercatinib in Pediatric and Adolescent Patients With RET-Altered Solid Tumors: Safety and Efficacy Results From the Phase I/II LIBRETTO-121 Study
items.authors: Laetsch TW, Kang HJ, Casanova M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Selpercatinib, a highly selective oral RET inhibitor with CNS activity, has previously demonstrated durable responses and an acceptable safety profile in adults with RET-driven cancers. Consequently, the safety and efficacy of selpercatinib were investigated in pediatric/adolescent participants. Methods: LIBRETTO-121 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03899792) was a multicenter phase I/II trial of selpercatinib in participants age 0.5-21 years with advanced, RET-altered solid tumors. In phase I, the primary end point was safety, including dose-limiting toxicities. In phase II, the primary end point was objective response rate (ORR) as determined by independent review committee (IRC) per RECIST v1.1. Key secondary end points included ORR by investigator, duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival, overall survival, safety, and pharmacokinetics. Results: As of November 8, 2024, 36 participants age 2-20 years were treated with selpercatinib. Tumor types included RET-altered medullary thyroid cancer (MTC, n = 15), RET fusion-positive papillary thyroid cancer (PTC, n = 15), and other (n = 6). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were diarrhea, nausea, elevated AST, pyrexia, abdominal pain, elevated ALT, headache, cough, and vomiting. No treatment discontinuations due to treatment-related adverse events or new adverse drug reactions were observed. ORR by IRC was 53% (19/36; 95% CI, 36 to 70). For participants with MTC and PTC, ORR by IRC was 60% (9/15; 95% CI, 32 to 84) and 53% (8/15; 95% CI, 27 to 79), respectively. The 24-month DOR rate was 100% (95% CI, 100 to 100). Conclusion: Selpercatinib showed durable efficacy in pediatric/adolescent participants with RET-altered thyroid cancer and was well tolerated, supporting targeting of RET alterations in pediatric/adolescent patients.

items.title: Patient preferences and travel burden before radiotherapy for primary cutaneous lymphoma: baseline results from the S-MISR registry
items.authors: Steike DR, Elsayad K, Falke I, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Patients with primary cutaneous lymphoma may have substantial impairments in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and may require referral to specialized radiation oncology centers. The current exploratory baseline analysis assessed patient preferences for quality of life (QoL) versus length of life (LoL), travel distance, and baseline HRQoL before radiotherapy. Methods: Of 130 screened patients, 82 patients with primary cutaneous lymphoma referred for radiotherapy were enrolled in the prospective S‑MISR registry between September 2019 and August 2024. Their QoL-versus-LoL preferences were assessed using the Quality-Quantity Questionnaire. Baseline HRQoL was evaluated using Skindex-29 and EORTC QLQ-C30. Travel distance to the treating radiation oncology department was analyzed overall and by lymphoma subtype. Results: Median age was 63 years (range 34-92), and 59 patients (72%) had advanced-stage disease. Fifty-six patients (68%) had mycosis fungoides (MF), 13 (16%) had Sézary syndrome (SS), and 13 (16%) had other primary cutaneous lymphomas. Overall, 31 patients (38%) prioritized QoL, 21 (25%) prioritized LoL, and 30 (37%) rated both equally. Median travel distance was longest for Sézary syndrome (201 km), followed by mycosis fungoides (114 km) and non-MF/SS lymphomas (65 km). Older age and longer travel distance emerged as potential factors associated with QoL preference. Baseline Skindex-29 scores indicated greater HRQoL impairment in MF and SS than in non-MF/SS lymphomas. Conclusion: Patient preferences regarding QoL versus LoL vary considerably before radiotherapy. Travel burden may be an important patient-centered factor for treatment planning, shared decision-making, and future prospective radiotherapy studies.

items.title: Device-Free Auricular Acupressure for Rosacea: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Xu B, Chu J, Wang Y, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation is effective for rosacea. However, its neuroimmunomodulatory effects lack sham-controlled serum biochemical evidence, and specialized device reliance limits its clinical popularization. Objective: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of device-free auricular acupressure for rosacea and verify its neuroimmunomodulatory effects using serum biomarkers and immediate vascular imaging in a sham-controlled trial. Design, Setting, And Participants: This single-center, randomized, sham-controlled, assessor-masked trial was conducted in the Dermatology Outpatient Department of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University from October 2025 to May 2026 and included 204 patients with rosacea who were receiving standard first-line treatment. Participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio using block randomization. Data analysis was initiated in May 2026. Interventions: The active acupressure group received a Vaccaria segetalis seed on the bilateral cavum conchae (innervated by the auricular vagus branch), while the sham group received a seed on the auricular tubercle superior margin (pure somatosensory innervation). Participants performed acupressure 3 times daily for 30 seconds, with extra pressing allowed during acute flare-ups. The intervention lasted 8 weeks. Serum levels of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (LL-37), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), and interleukin (IL) 6 were measured at baseline and week 8. Multispectral imaging was performed at baseline and week 4 to assess immediate vascular responses. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was treatment success, defined as an Investigator Global Assessment (IGA) score of 0 or 1 at week 8. The number needed to treat was calculated from absolute risk difference. Results: The 204 participants were equally divided into 2 groups (102 each; active acupressure: mean [SD] age, 32.51 [10.60] years, 86 female individuals [84.3%]; sham acupressure: mean [SD] age, 30.82 [9.32] years, 86 female individuals [84.3%]). At week 8, the active acupressure group had a higher IGA success rate (58 [56.9%] vs 36 [35.3%]; relative risk, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.18-2.20; P = .003; number needed to treat, 5). Serum LL-37, CGRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 levels decreased more significantly in the active acupressure group. The immediate vascular improvement rate was 59.3% vs 7.4% (P < .001). At week 20, the active acupressure group maintained significantly lower IGA and Clinical Erythema Assessment scores.…

items.title: American Society of Hematology 2026 Guidelines for the Management of Myelofibrosis in Adults
items.authors: Stein BL, Abdallah MM, Abel GA, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Myelofibrosis (MF) is a myeloid bone marrow malignancy with a progressive clinical course marked by disease-related symptoms, splenomegaly, cytopenias, thrombosis/hemorrhage, and a risk for blast phase transformation. Treatment recommendations are based on the burden of symptoms, prognosis of the disease, and benefits/risks of each treatment modality. Methods: ASH formed a multidisciplinary guideline panel that included specialists in myelofibrosis and hematopoietic cell transplantation, as well 2 patient representatives and was balanced to minimize potential bias from conflicts of interest. The Mayo Clinic Evidence-based Practice Center supported the guideline development process, including updating or performing systematic evidence reviews (up to January 31, 2025). The panel prioritized clinical questions and outcomes according to their importance for patients and clinicians. The panel used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, including GRADE Evidence-to-Decision frameworks, to assess evidence and make recommendations, which were subject to public comment. Results: The panel agreed on 10 recommendations regarding prognostic testing, indications for interferon and JAK inhibitor therapy, management of MF-associated anemia, timing of transplantation, anti-platelet therapy, and iron chelation. Conclusions: Key recommendations of these guidelines include suggestions for extended molecular genetic testing; use of JAK-inhibition in symptomatic, lower risk MF patients; therapeutic strategies for patients with MF-anemia and JAK-inhibitor induced anemia; and considerations regarding hematopoietic cell transplantation including timing of referral and optimization prior to the procedure. Key future research agendas were identified for all recommendations.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of camrelizumab plus docetaxel and carboplatin as neoadjuvant therapy for stage II-III triple-negative breast cancer: the HELEN-Trio 011 randomized clinical trial
items.authors: Jiao D, Sun X, Qiao J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy has become the standard-of-care for stage II-III triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC); however, anthracycline-containing regimens are associated with considerable toxicity. We evaluated camrelizumab combined with an anthracycline-free docetaxel-carboplatin regimen in this setting. Patients And Methods: We performed a multicenter, randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial at 14 hospitals in China between December 2022 and June 2025. Eligible patients were women aged 18-70 years with previously untreated, stage II-III TNBC. Patients were randomized 2:1 to receive 6 cycles of neoadjuvant docetaxel (75 mg/m2) plus carboplatin (area under the curve [AUC]=6) on day 1, with or without camrelizumab (200 mg intravenously on day 3). The primary endpoint was pathological complete response (pCR), defined as ypT0/Tis ypN0, evaluated in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population (all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment). Results: A total of 369 patients were enrolled, and 352 comprised the mITT population for efficacy analysis. The pCR rate was 57.5% (134/233) in the camrelizumab-chemotherapy group and 45.4% (54/119) in the chemotherapy-alone group, corresponding to an absolute difference of 12.2% (95% CI, 1.4 to 22.9; one-sided P=0.014). Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 24.9% (58/233) in the camrelizumab-chemotherapy group and 21.8% (26/119) in the chemotherapy-alone group. No treatment-related deaths were reported. Conclusion: The addition of camrelizumab to neoadjuvant docetaxel plus carboplatin significantly increased the pCR rate in patients with stage II-III TNBC, with a manageable safety profile. This regimen represents a promising anthracycline-free strategy that warrants comparison with current standard chemoimmunotherapy .

items.title: EGFR-targeted antibody-toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial
items.authors: Chandramohan V, Herndon JE 2nd, Barnwal A, et al.
items.abstract: D2C7-ATC is a recombinant antibody-toxin conjugate (ATC) targeting wild-type epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mutant EGFR variant III (EGFRvIII). We conducted a single-arm, single-site, open-label phase 1 trial evaluating a single infusion of D2C7-ATC via convection-enhanced delivery in the enhancing disease of 81 patients with biopsy-confirmed recurrent malignant glioma. The primary objective was to determine toxicity and the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of D2C7-ATC. Secondary objectives included describing overall survival (OS) and assessing the association between EGFR expression and OS. The median overall survival (mOS) was 7.9 months among 72 patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type recurrent glioblastoma (IDHwt rGBM), including 35 patients in the dose-escalation stage (40 to 35,032 ng ml-1) and 37 patients in the dose-expansion stage (RP2D of 6,920 ng ml-1). D2C7-ATC was generally well tolerated, with mainly grade 1-2 treatment-related adverse events (67%). The maximum tolerated dose was exceeded at 35,032 ng ml-1, where four patients experienced dose-limiting toxicities, including grade 4 (N = 2) and grade 3 (N = 2) events. Eight patients died on trial; all deaths were unrelated to D2C7-ATC. Univariate analyses identified survival-associated biomarkers, including tumor D2C7 antibody reactivity, circulating cytokines, a tumor inflammatory gene signature and neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes in blood. Notably, patients with IDHwt rGBM with a D2C7 antibody reactivity score of <1.5+ in pre-treatment tumor had an mOS of 17.38 months, whereas those with low IL-8 in post-treatment plasma had an mOS of 16.6 months. These findings indicate that EGFR-targeted D2C7-ATC therapy prolongs survival in a subset of patients with IDHwt rGBM via intratumoral and systemic immune activation. items.title: Efficient deep learning-driven workflows for accelerated single-fraction radiation therapy planning of a solitary tumour in the lung
items.authors: Gaudreault M, Hardcastle N, Woodford K, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Same-day, single-fraction radiotherapy requires efficient planning. We introduce two deep learning (DL) dose prediction-driven workflows to generate clinically acceptable plans for treating metastases in the lung. Materials And Methods: Consecutive patients treated for a tumour in the lung (11/2018-11/2024) were considered. One workflow used the computed tomography density map and a synthetic dose built from the tumour segmentation as inputs for the DL model [without-organs of interest (OOI)]. The other workflow additionally used predicted OOI segmentations (with-OOI). Optimisation objectives were extracted from the predicted dose by the treatment planning system (TPS). Generated plans were compared with clinical plans with the number of achieved goals, conformity index CI100, and control point modulation complexity score (cpMCS). Plan complexity increases with decreasing cpMCS. Processing times were recorded. Results: Training and testing datasets contained 200 and 56 treatments, respectively. Without- / with-OOI workflows generated plans in 8.8 and 9.6 min. The 3%/3 mm gamma passing rates between predicted and clinical doses were median ± interquartile range 99.4 ± 0.7% / 99.3 ± 0.8%. After dose optimisation in the TPS, 25% of plans had a higher number of achieved clinical goals relative to clinical plans in both workflows. The conformity was improved (CI100 = -5.3% / -3.9% relative to the clinical value, p-values <0.001) at the cost of increased complexity (cpMCS = -19.4% / -19.0%, p-values <0.001). Conclusions: Workflows driven by DL dose prediction could generate a clinically acceptable plan in less than ten minutes for same-day, single-fraction treatment of a tumour in the lung.

items.title: Design, Customization, and Implementation of an Oncology Information System-Based Paperless Proton Therapy Workflow
items.authors: Raveendran V, Darekar K, Sinha S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Proton therapy centers present distinctive workflow challenges that demand seamless coordination, documentation, and collaboration across multidisciplinary teams. Given the limited published experience with paperless workflows in proton therapy, this study describes the design, customization, and 2-year clinical implementation of a comprehensive paperless workflow at a newly commissioned multi-room proton therapy center using a commercial oncology information system (OIS). Methods: A multidisciplinary team of radiation oncologists, medical physicists, and radiotherapy technologists led the development and implementation of a department-wide paperless workflow with the Elekta MOSAIQ OIS. The process followed a structured 5-phase strategy and leveraged native OIS functionalities, including Quality Control Lists (QCLs) for task management, virtual locations, IQ Scripts for automation, customized assessment forms, and eScribe templates. User acceptance was evaluated via a multidisciplinary satisfaction survey conducted 26 months post-implementation. Results: The paperless workflow covered the entire patient pathway, from pre-planning audit to treatment completion and discharge summary generation, and incorporated 22 QCLs, 13 virtual locations, 44 IQ scripts, 10 customized assessment forms, and 2 eScribe templates. Implementation reduced the reliance on paper, improved workflow traceability, standardized multidisciplinary approvals, reduced missed tasks, and enhanced interdisciplinary coordination. A 3-tier physics plan review process ensured safety and quality assurance in treatment planning and evaluation while reducing variability among planners. The satisfaction survey (n = 36) yielded an overall mean score of 3.79/5.0, with safety and quality rated highest (3.87/5.0), while system usability identified opportunities for future optimization (3.53/5.0). Conclusions: A fully paperless, OIS-driven proton therapy workflow was designed and successfully implemented using the native capabilities of the MOSAIQ OIS system. The structured, multidisciplinary approach and proton-specific checklist framework presented here provide a practical and reproducible model for other centers establishing particle therapy programs.

items.title: Feasibility of ultra-low-field MRI in an ion beam treatment room for online MR-guided particle therapy
items.authors: Pfitzer J, Scharfetter H, Antypas P, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Online MR-guided particle therapy may improve beam delivery precision and treatment efficacy. Ultra-low-field (ULF) MRI may enable image guidance with minimal modification of existing facilities. The feasibility of operating a ULF magnetic resonance (MR) scanner for online MR-guided particle therapy in an unmodified ion-beam therapy environment was investigated. Material And Methods: A portable 49 mT ULF-MRI system (OSI2 ONE MR scanner) was placed at the isocenter of a research room at an ion-beam therapy facility without radio-frequency shielding. Image quality was assessed using a grid phantom under static and dynamic irradiation conditions for protons and carbon ions. Electromagnetic interference (EMI) was characterized and mitigated via grounding and local shielding. Beam deflections were quantified using a scintillation detector and compared to numerical simulations. The impact of ongoing proton and carbon ion irradiation on the imaging process was assessed. Dosimetric measurements were performed using a Semiflex ionization chamber in a PMMA phantom with and without simultaneous MR imaging. Results: Stable image quality was achieved across proton and carbon ion irradiation with no relevant irradiation-induced artifacts. Initially substantial EMI was reduced to near-baseline levels by internal shielding. Proton beam deflections ranged from 0.9-1.7 mm at isocenter, consistent with simulations. Dosimetric deviations were below 0.05% for 2D fields and 0.02% for spread-out Bragg peaks (SOBP). Conclusion: ULF-MRI operation in an ion-beam therapy environment without a dedicated shielded room is feasible, without compromising imaging, beam delivery, or dosimetry. This approach supports future MR-guided particle therapy research with reduced infrastructural requirements.
