items.title: Cone beam computed tomography guided online adaptive radiotherapy for cervical Cancer: Two-year single-Centre implementation and clinical experience
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Barten DLJ, Goudschaal K, Hinnen KA, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Managing inter- and intrafraction motion remains a major challenge in cervical cancer radiotherapy. This study reports a two-year, single-centre experience with daily CBCT-guided cervical online adaptive radiotherapy (oART), evaluating the workflow feasibility of a radiation therapist (RTT)-led adaptive workflow, including treatment session duration and target coverage. Materials And Methods: Thirty patients with cervical cancer were treated with CBCT-guided oART between October 2023 and December 2025. After initial supervised sessions, treatment delivery transitioned to an RTT-led workflow supported by a traffic-light protocol with on-call multidisciplinary backup. Cervical oART was introduced in phases, progressing from single-isocentre cases to more complex treatments including two isocentres and para-aortic lymph nodes. Workflow evaluation was based on retrospective analysis of session logs, process timing and oART workflow-related interventions. Results: A total of 744 adaptive sessions were analysed. Median total session duration was 33.0 min (interquartile range 13.0). Imaging and beam delivery times were stable, whereas decision-intensive steps showed greater variability, requiring corrections to AI-generated contours in all patients. Median total session duration was comparable between the first five supervised sessions and the subsequent RTT-led sessions (32.5 vs. 32.0 min). Contour review showed the strongest correlation with total session duration (ρ = 0.73). Uterus displacement outside the PTV due to intrafraction motion was observed in approximately 11% of all post-treatment CBCT-verifications and was typically limited to small fundal regions. Conclusion: Daily CBCT-guided cervical oART can be efficiently implemented within an RTT-led workflow, demonstrating workflow feasibility while maintaining target coverage despite intra-fraction anatomical variability.

items.title: 3D analysis and evolution of prostate and tumor oxygenation using MRI-derived relative oxygen extraction fraction during MR-guided stereotactic body radiotherapy
items.authors: Berger T, Lapierre A, Zidane P, et al.
items.abstract: Background/Purpose: Tumor hypoxia is a major cause of radioresistance, motivating the development of biomarkers related to tissue oxygen physiology that can be monitored throughout treatment. MRI-derived relative Oxygen Extraction Fraction (rOEF) is a non-invasive imaging biomarker related to tissue oxygen extraction. This study characterized the temporal evolution of rOEF during MR-guided stereotactic body radiotherapy (MRgSBRT) for prostate cancer. Materials/Methods: Twenty-three prostate cancer patients treated with five-fraction MRgSBRT were analyzed. rOEF maps were acquired at treatment planning and at each treatment fraction. Average rOEF was extracted from the healthy prostate, gross tumor volume (GTV), and two gluteal muscle regions receiving either residual (in-field) or negligible (out-of-field) irradiation. Longitudinal changes in average rOEF and in the fraction of GTV voxels with rOEF >70% were quantified using patient-specific linear fits. Slopes of average rOEF in the healthy prostate were also calculated between successive imaging sessions. Results: Average rOEF decreased significantly in all irradiated regions (healthy prostate, GTV and in-field gluteal muscle), with no significant change in the out-of-field gluteal muscle. The fraction of GTV voxels with rOEF >70% also declined significantly. In the healthy prostate, rOEF decreased predominantly during the first four fractions, with the steepest median slope observed between planning and the first treatment fraction (-3.2). Conclusions: MRgSBRT was associated with a progressive reduction in rOEF confined to irradiated tissues, with the largest decrease in healthy prostate rOEF occurring after the first irradiation. These findings suggest rOEF could be a potential imaging biomarker of physiological changes associated with radiation exposure and warrant further investigation of its relationship with physiological processes and tissue hypoxia.

items.title: Prediction of radiation-induced hypothyroidism after proton-based supraclavicular nodal irradiation in breast cancer
items.authors: Sun J, Li P, Hao Y, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The thyroid gland lies adjacent to the supraclavicular target and is highly radiosensitive, placing patients at risk for radiation‐induced hypothyroidism (RIHT). While RIHT incidence and predictive models have been well described after photon‐based irradiation, evidence in the proton therapy setting remains limited. Purpose To evaluate the incidence of RIHT in breast cancer patients undergoing proton‐based supraclavicular nodal irradiation and to develop proton‐specific normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models incorporating dose‐volume, dose‐averaged linear energy transfer (LETd)‐volume, and dose–LETd–volume histogram (DLVH) metrics. Methods A total of 113 breast cancer patients treated with proton supraclavicular irradiation were retrospectively analyzed. Dose‐volume, LETd‐volume, and DLVH metrics were extracted for the thyroid gland and individual thyroid lobes. After exclusion of non‐informative variables, univariable logistic regression models were developed for all retained candidate predictors. Internal validation and model selection were performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples, and the final bootstrap‐selected predictor was defined as the variable with the highest selection frequency. Model performance was assessed using apparent and optimism‐corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Biological dose metrics were additionally generated using six published LET‐dependent relative biological effectiveness (RBE) models and compared with the fixed‐RBE model using paired DeLong tests. Results Seventeen patients (15.0%) developed RIHT after a median follow‐up of 25 months (range, 9–80 months). Under the fixed‐RBE framework, the final bootstrap‐selected predictors were complementary DLVH metrics: CD10L2 (cc), denoting the absolute volume not simultaneously receiving dose ≥ 10 Gy(RBE) and LETd ≥ 2 keV/µm, CD35L3 (cc), and CD5L4 (cc) for the thyroid gland, ipsilateral lobe, and contralateral lobe, respectively. The corresponding apparent AUCs were 0.794, 0.763, and 0.817, with optimism‐corrected AUCs of 0.738, 0.708, and 0.766, respectively. Among the LET‐dependent RBE models, the Wedenberg model based on contralateral lobe CD10L4 (cc) yielded the numerically highest optimism‐corrected AUC of 0.772. Although LET‐dependent RBE models showed slightly higher apparent AUCs than the fixed‐RBE model in some analyses, paired DeLong tests did not demonstrate statistically significant differences. Conclusions RIHT is a clinically relevant toxicity after proton‐based supraclavicular irradiation.…

items.title: Evaluation of online dose-guided adaptive fractionation for intact prostate radiotherapy
items.authors: Gevorkyan GS, Zhu L, Tegtmeier RC, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Dose-guided adaptive fractionation (DGAF) was proposed as a simpler alternative of adaptive radiation therapy, using organ variation simulation for proof of concept. However, its dosimetric benefit using actual daily anatomy changes in prostate cancer patients remains unclear. Purpose: The purpose of this study was to retrospectively evaluate the dosimetric benefit and potential risk of DGAF for prostate cancer patients treated with moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy using daily cone-beam CT. Methods: Patients assessed in this study were treated with moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy (MHRT, n = 11, 244 total fractions) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT, n = 11, 55 total fractions). The optimizer algorithm computed the desired fractional dose based on favorable or unfavorable anatomical conditions derived from daily imaging, quantified by the sparing factor threshold (μ) and spread (σ). Three methods of estimating subsequent fractionation schemes were explored. The assessment relative to patient-specific probabilities observed post-treatment includes the cohort-based probability (CBP) approach, the individual-based probability (IBP) approach, and the hybrid approach that begins as CBP and transitions to the IBP after a certain number of fractions. The benefits/risks of DGAF were assessed by calculating the equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2) for both the CTV and the rectum in comparison to regular fractionation. Results: DGAF demonstrated potential dosimetric benefits for intact prostate patients. The average and standard deviation of the sparing factor was 0.51 ± 0.11 for MHRT patients and 0.42 ± 0.04 for SBRT patients treated with endorectal-balloon. The hybrid approach for estimating the patients' threshold μ and spread σ outperformed other approaches assessed for both cohorts. The highest dosimetric benefit was retrospectively seen in MHRT patients where a hybrid approach were used, showing equal or decreased D15% EQD2. Conclusion: DGAF demonstrated considerable rectum sparing potential, and the benefits increased with longer fractionation and advanced approaches toward subsequent fraction estimation.

items.title: Omission of lateral isocenter shifts in robust optimization of proton therapy treatment plans for prostate cancer
items.authors: O'Grady FT, Castro J, Kim DW, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Proton therapy is routinely used to treat prostate cancer using bilaterally opposed beams and can achieve lower dose to nearby organs-at-risk (OARs) such as the bladder and rectum. Pencil beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy offers the most conformal treatment plans to best spare healthy tissue. Robust optimization is often utilized in planning PBS treatment to account for uncertainties in treatment delivery, such as misalignment of the isocenter, by evaluating the dose in perturbation scenarios in which the isocenter is translated. This process is effective but resource intensive and time consuming. Purpose: To assess the feasibility of omitting lateral translations of the isocenter in robust optimization of pencil-beam scanning (PBS) proton therapy treatment plans for prostate cancer patients, utilizing parallel opposed lateral beams. Methods: The impact of isocenter shifts in the beam direction was studied systematically in a series of cube plans of varying field size and depth in water. In addition, the impact of omitting lateral isocenter shifts in robust optimization was analyzed retrospectively across sixteen clinical treatment plans, including plans with pelvic lymph nodes (LN) and a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB) delivered to the dominant intraprostatic lesion (DIL) or PET avid LNs. The impact on key dose-volume metrics for several OARs, as well as the results of robust evaluation and the difference in optimization time were recorded. Results: The plan comparison shows no significant difference in dose to any OAR or robust target coverage for any of the plans considered. The time required for a single optimization with fixed settings reduced by 24 min (22%) on average, with a maximum reduction of 129 min (43.1%). Conclusions: Lateral isocenter shifts can be safely omitted in robust optimization of PBS proton therapy treatment plans for prostate patients, utilizing parallel opposed lateral beams, to achieve a significant reduction in optimization time, without increasing dose to OARs or sacrificing robust target coverage.

items.title: Cervical Cancer Screening Rates by Race and Ethnicity, Age, Language, and Census Region
items.authors: Xie Y, Nguyen L, Le YC, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Longitudinal evidence of cervical cancer screening (CCS) trends before and after COVID-19 across demographic cohorts remains limited. Objective: To examine CCS rates by race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region among patients with at least 1 health care encounter in an electronic medical record (EMR) system from 2019 through 2024, and to evaluate longitudinal trends across these groups. Design, Setting, And Participants: Using an EMR database, this cross-sectional study evaluated CCS rates among female patients aged 21 to 64 years between 2019 and 2024, stratified by race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region. Exposures: Race and ethnicity, age, language, and census region. Main Outcomes And Measures: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize annual CCS rates across demographic groups. The Cochran-Armitage test assessed linear trends over time. Results: Annual sample sizes ranged from approximately 9 to 16 million patients and increased steadily over time; analytic population sizes varied across subgroups. Most patients were non-Hispanic White, aged 30 to 49 years, English-speaking, and resided in either the South or Northeast. Non-Hispanic White patients had the highest annual CCS rates from 2019 to 2021 but experienced the smallest percentage increase, from 10.98% (95% CI, 10.96%-11.01%) to 13.85% (95% CI, 13.82%-13.87%), over the study period. Hispanic patients experienced the largest percentage increase in CCS rates, from 9.85% (95% CI, 9.80%-9.90%) to 15.51% (95% CI, 15.47%-15.55%). American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander patients had the lowest screening rates throughout the study period. Patients aged 30 to 49 years and non-English-speaking patients consistently had the highest CCS rates across all years. Patients in the Western and Southern census regions had lower CCS rates than those in other regions. Conclusions And Relevance: In this cross-sectional study of patients with at least 1 health care encounter in an EMR system, all CCS rates increased across all racial and ethnic groups from 2019 to 2024, with the greatest gains observed among Hispanic patients. However, persistent disparities remained, particularly among American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander patients and those in the Western and Southern regions. These findings suggest that although screening uptake has improved over time, substantial geographic and racial and ethnic disparities in CCS persist, highlighting important areas for future research and intervention efforts.

items.title: Trigger-based adaptive proton therapy and changes in target coverage and cardiac dose in esophageal cancer
items.authors: Badiu V, Kneepkens E, Reijtenbagh D, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Inter-fractional anatomical variations during proton therapy for esophageal cancer may compromise target coverage and increase dose to surrounding organs. Adaptive replanning can mitigate these effects, but its cumulative dose-based and clinical impact remains insufficiently characterized. We evaluated offline adaptive intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) triggered by target underdose or cardiac overdose using deformable dose accumulation. Materials And Methods: A retrospective cohort of 192 esophageal cancer patients treated with IMPT was analyzed. Eighty-five underwent adaptive replanning and 107 were treated non-adaptively. Dose accumulation was performed by assigning each fraction to the closest weekly repeat computed tomography (CT) scan and deformably mapping doses to the planning CT. Accumulated doses from adapted and non-adapted plans were compared for internal target volume (ITV) and gross tumor volume (GTV) coverage, target hotspots, heart and lung dose, and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) for 2-year post-treatment mortality. Results: Compared with the non-adaptive treatment scenario, the adaptive scenario increased ITV D98% by 1.9 percentage points (pp) and GTV D98% by 0.8 pp. in the target underdose subgroup. In the cardiac overdose subgroup, mean heart dose decreased by 1.0 Gy and heart V40Gy by 1.7 pp., with no increase in mean lung dose. NTCP for 2-year post-treatment mortality decreased by 1.5 pp. in this subgroup. Conclusions: Trigger-based adaptive IMPT improved cumulative target coverage and cardiac sparing without increasing lung dose. Target underdose and cardiac overdose triggers provided complementary benefits, supporting their use in structured adaptive replanning.

items.title: Incremental Value of Radiation Dose for Prognostic Stratification Beyond Performance Status in Palliative Radiation Therapy for Bone Metastases
items.authors: Watanabe Y, Tomoda T, Iwata A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Although the individual prognostic value of performance status (PS) and prescribed dose for overall survival (OS) in palliative radiation therapy for bone metastases has been investigated, their combined prognostic significance has not been thoroughly explored. This study aimed to evaluate the combined prognostic value of PS and prescribed dose for OS in patients with bone metastases undergoing palliative radiation therapy. Methods And Materials: This study included 423 patients who underwent palliative radiation therapy for bone metastases between January 2013 and October 2024. The primary endpoint was OS, evaluated at fixed follow-up points of 1, 3, and 6 months, as well as 1, 2, and 3 years. Results: Univariate Cox regression analysis demonstrated that 1-year OS was significantly associated with poor PS (hazard ratio, 2.6 [95% CI, 2.2-3.1]; P < .001) and a lower prescribed dose (<39 Gy in a biologically effective dose with α/β = 10; hazard ratio, 3.9 [95% CI, 2.8-5.3]; P < .001), both of which remained independent predictors of worse OS in multivariate analysis (both P < .001). Comparison of the areas under the curves showed that adding prescribed dose to PS significantly improved the predictive accuracy of OS at 1 and 3 months (both P < .001), 6 months (P = .002), 1 year (P = .028), and 2 years (P = .032). However, the improvement was not statistically significant at 3 years (P = .086). Kaplan-Meier curve analysis with log-rank tests showed that combining PS and prescribed dose improved OS risk stratification (P < .001 for all follow-up periods), regardless of primary tumor risk or the number of distant metastases. Conclusions: Combining PS and prescribed dose enabled more refined risk stratification for predicting short- and long-term OS in patients with bone metastases undergoing palliative radiation therapy, regardless of primary tumor risk classification or the number of distant metastases. Moreover, adding prescribed dose to PS provided significant incremental predictive value for OS in this setting.

items.title: Evaluation of the nutritional and digestive impact of irradiation in nasopharyngeal cancers: the French multicenter retrospective DRAKAR study
items.authors: Cochin T, Le Guévelou J, Thariat J, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Radiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancers is associated with frequent digestive and nutritional toxicities, weight loss (WL), and malnutrition, criteria of poor tolerance and poor prognosis. The primary objective of DRAKAR was to evaluate the effect of prophylactic enteral nutrition (EN) on weight change (WC) during, at the end of, and after radiotherapy in patients with nasopharyngeal cancer from a non-endemic French population. Materials And Methods: DRAKAR is a retrospective, multicenter study conducted in five French centers. Patients received radiotherapy with curative intent, with or without concurrent chemotherapy, for primary nasopharyngeal cancer between 2015 and 2024. The primary endpoint was WC according to nutritional support modality at the end of radiotherapy. Secondary endpoints included rates of moderate and severe malnutrition (5% or 10% WL in one month for moderate and severe malnutrition), grade ≥ 3 toxicities, dosimetry parameters (volumes, particles), use and duration of EN and parenteral nutrition, prolonged radiotherapy due to treatment interruption, hospitalizations, and overall survival. Results: Among the 124 patients analyzed (59.7% UCNT, 40.3% squamous cell carcinoma), mean WC was -6.45% at the end of radiotherapy. At one month, 35.5% were malnourished, compared with 8% before treatment. EN was used in 55.6% of patients, including 16.1% prophylactically. Prophylactic EN was associated with stabilization of WC after treatment. Regarding malnutrition, age < 55 years was the only significant clinical factor associated with its occurrence, with no association found with toxicity, dosimetric, or therapeutic characteristics. Conclusion: In patients treated for nasopharyngeal cancer, prophylactic EN was associated with post-treatment WC stabilization but not with hospitalization or improved survival. Given potential confounding by indication, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, and prospective studies are needed to confirm the benefit and optimal indications for prophylactic EN.

items.title: Feasibility of longitudinal prostate R(2) (⁎) measurements in patients undergoing stereotactic ablative radiotherapy on an MRI-linac
items.authors: Moore C, Ezekiel A, Bamunuarachchi V, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Tissue R2* (1/T2*), sensitive to deoxyhaemoglobin, is a proposed hypoxia biomarker in prostate cancer. This exploratory work investigates prostate R2* and volume throughout and after hypo-fractionated radiotherapy and the effects of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Materials And Methods: Fifteen patients (seven with ADT) received five-fraction stereotactic-ablative-radiotherapy (SABR) on a 1.5 T Elekta Unity MRI-linac, with R2* mapping at MR-Simulation and treatment visits 1, 3, 5. Six patients had follow-up imaging post-treatment.Treatment-induced whole-prostate and tumour R2*/volume differences were investigated using repeated-measures analysis-of-variance.ADT effects on baseline whole-prostate R2*/volume were investigated using unpaired t-tests. Spearman correlations between whole-prostate R2* and volume were calculated before and during treatment. Results: Whole-prostate R2* (mean difference [95% CIs] = -1.77 [-2.17 to -0.498] s-1, p = 0.003) and tumour R2* (-3.11 [-5.78 to -1.44] s-1, p = 0.003) decreased, whole-prostate volume (8.05 [4.76 to 11.7] cm3) increased after two fractions.Follow-up whole-prostate R2* (p = 0.62) and volume (p = 0.16) were not significantly different from baseline.ADT patients had higher baseline whole-prostate R2* (p = 0.006) and lower volume (p = 0.003). ADT did not impact treatment-induced changes (p = 0.51).Baseline whole-prostate R2*/volume were negatively correlated (r = -0.75, p = 0.002); treatment-induced R2*/volume changes were not correlated r = 0.44, p = 0.11). Conclusions: Treatment-induced whole-prostate and tumour R2* changes were measured after two SABR fractions. Post-treatment whole-prostate R2* and volume were not significantly different from baseline.Further work is required to confirm the mechanism(s) causing observed treatment effects.

items.title: Effects of Isthmus-Sparing Lobectomy on Thyroid Function: A Prospective, Multicenter, Comparative Study
items.authors: Kim WW, Jeon YS, Cho J, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background This prospective study evaluated the impact of isthmus management (isthmus‐sparing vs. isthmus‐removing lobectomy) on postoperative hypothyroidism risk. Methods Between January 2022 and March 2023, 326 euthyroid patients with benign or low‐risk papillary thyroid cancer were randomized into the isthmus‐sparing (IS, n = 164) or isthmus‐removing (IR, n = 162) group. Administration of levothyroxine was limited to patients with overt hypothyroidism or symptomatic subclinical hypothyroidism. Results TSH levels were significantly lower in the IS group at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months (p<0.05$$ p<0.05 $$). Euthyroidism maintenance was higher in the IS group (62.2% vs. 38.9%, p=0.001$$ p=0.001 $$). The IS group showed lower subclinical hypothyroidism (33.8% vs. 54.9%, p=0.001$$ p=0.001 $$) and hormone replacement rates (8.5% vs. 25.3%, p=0.001$$ p=0.001 $$). Overt hypothyroidism was lower in the IS group without statistical significance (6.1% vs. 12.3%, p=0.057$$ p=0.057 $$). Conclusion Isthmus‐sparing lobectomy better preserves thyroid function and reduces postoperative subclinical hypothyroidism and hormone replacement needs compared to isthmus‐removing lobectomy.

items.title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review
items.authors: Chen D, Blayne A, Ning T, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design: Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data Sources: Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility Criteria: Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main Outcome Measures: Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results: The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time.…

items.title: Risk of second primary malignancies in older long-term survivors of breast, prostate, colon, and rectal cancer
items.authors: Kwaramba T, Westvold S, Long JB, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Cancer survivors face an increased risk of second primary malignancies (SPMs). Understanding SPM incidence and risk factors is crucial for long-term survivorship care. Methods: This was a SEER-Medicare retrospective cohort study of breast, prostate, colon, or rectal cancer survivors diagnosed between 2003-2011 at age 66+ years who survived ≥5 years post-diagnosis. The primary outcome was a 'late' SPM, defined as invasive cancer occurring ≥5 years after initial diagnosis. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) regression was used to assess demographic, clinical, and treatment related factors associated with late SPMs. SPMs were categorized as hematologic, screen-detectable (breast, prostate, lung, colon, or rectal), or non-screen detectable solid tumors. Results: Of 90,261 long-term survivors, 11.2% (10,116) developed at least one late SPM. The cumulative incidence of late SPMs over 8 years was highest in prostate cancer survivors. Non-screen detectable cancers composed the largest proportion (47.8%) of 10,220 total late SPMs. The most common late SPM site was lung in colon (14.9%), and rectal (16.1%) cancer survivors, urinary bladder in prostate (17.0%), and new-primary breast cancers in breast cancer survivors (36.5%). In RMST regression, significant associations with demographic, index cancer, treatment, and clinical characteristics and late SPMs ranged from 3.6 months shorter to 4.4 months longer time without late SPM during the 8 years assessed. Conclusions: Between 10-14% of older long-term cancer survivors developed a late SPM during 5-13 years after index cancer diagnosis. Over 40% of late SPMs were screen-detectable, highlighting the need for surveillance strategies beyond 5 years from index cancer diagnosis.

items.title: Neurodevelopmental Blueprint in Gliomas: Toward an Ontogenetic Multimodal Integrated Therapy
items.authors: Padevit L, Weiss T, Vasella F, et al.
items.abstract: Neuroepithelial tumors, including diffuse gliomas and embryonal neoplasms, remain among the most lethal cancers despite major advances in molecular diagnostics and some novel targeted therapies for subsets of patients. A persistent barrier to progress is the lack of a unifying framework that integrates their cellular hierarchy, spatial heterogeneity, and distinctive patterns of progression. In this review, we synthesize converging evidence that neuroepithelial tumor biology represents a pathologic re-enactment of brain ontogeny. Integrating molecular, single-cell, histoarchitectonic, and anatomic observations, we propose that neoplastic transformation, aberrant lineage commitment, and dedifferentiation mirror and invert physiological ontogenetic trajectories. This ontogenetic logic provides a coherent explanation for key hallmarks of neuroepithelial tumors, including intratumoral mosaicism, directional anatomic spread, and the emergence of therapy-resistant tumor-propagating cell states. Ontogenetic multimodal integrated therapy is an anatomy-guided strategy that aligns neurosurgery, radiotherapy, and pharmacotherapy with tumor stage and ontogenetic architecture. By shifting emphasis from radiologically visible tumor bulk to compartment-based developmental logic, this framework offers testable hypotheses and a clinically oriented paradigm for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring in patients with neuroepithelial tumors.

items.title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy for Management of Locally Advanced Periorbital Tumors: Efficacy and Toxicity Profile
items.authors: Ojo O, Gill K, Huang B, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The management of locally advanced periorbital skin tumors with orbital invasion is challenging. Orbital exenteration historically provides reliable local control but causes major functional and cosmetic morbidity. We evaluated stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as an eye‐sparing alternative, focusing on local control, vision preservation, and toxicity. Methods This retrospective series includes 26 consecutive patients with locally advanced periorbital tumors treated prospectively with SBRT. Tumors involved the canthi (zones III–IV) in 20 patients, with multi‐zone involvement in 18 and complete periorbital skin invasion (zone V) in 4. Eighteen tumors violated the orbital septum; anterior orbital invasion was observed in 16, and middle orbital invasion in 14. Extraconal violation occurred in 16 patients, and intraconal invasion in 15 patients. All patients were presented with intact ipsilateral vision at baseline. SBRT was delivered using VMAT/IMRT with a simultaneous integrated boost of 35–40 Gy to GTV and 25 Gy to CTV + 2 mm over five biweekly fractions. Optic apparatus constraints included Orbit PRV and Optic N PRV maximum point ≤ 30 Gy and mean ≤ 20 Gy; Lacrimal gland mean < 26 Gy when feasible. OAR constraints were based on institutional treatment directives supported by AAPM TG‐101, QUANTEC, and Emami et al. 50% received systemic therapy, including immunotherapy, targeted therapy, or chemotherapy, with some receiving combined approaches. Local and regional control and toxicities (CTCAE v5.0) were recorded; statistical analysis was primarily descriptive. Kaplan–Meier methodology was used to estimate local control and overall survival. Given the limited cohort size and heterogeneous tumor histologies, no formal comparative statistical testing was performed. Results Twenty‐four patients presented with primary cutaneous tumors and 2 had non‐cutaneous histologies (solitary fibrous tumor and metastatic breast carcinoma). SBRT was delivered as definitive therapy in 19 patients and as adjuvant therapy in 7. Median planning target volumes (PTVs) were 45 cc (PTV25) and 9 cc (PTV35–40 Gy), with corresponding median D90 values of 29 and 34/42 Gy, respectively. At a median follow‐up of 18 months (range 4–50 months), all patients retained intact vision. Twenty‐one patients achieved complete response, one had stable disease, and three experienced locoregional recurrences—one cavernous sinus failure and two local‐regional relapses.…

items.title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas
items.authors: Chowdhury T, Tesileanu CMS, Kocakavuk E, et al.
items.abstract: Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas that most commonly arise in adults under the age of 50 and exhibit variable responses to treatment1-3. To understand the genetic drivers of disease progression, here we used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to characterize longitudinally collected tumour specimens from 183 patients with IDH-mutant glioma. Samples were collected through the Glioma Longitudinal Analysis (GLASS) Consortium4. Most primary surgery samples were classified as grade 2 on the basis of histology (73% for astrocytomas and 93% for oligodendrogliomas). We validated known genomic markers of tumour progression, including hypermutation and homozygous deletion of CDKN2A or CDKN2B (hereafter, CDKN2A/B)5, and discovered genetic alterations that distinguish between the evolutionary trajectories of astrocytomas and those of oligodendrogliomas. Mutations in phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and NOTCH1 were newly acquired in recurrent oligodendrogliomas, regardless of treatment, and were associated with an increased tumour mutational burden. In recurrent astrocytomas, however, again irrespective of treatment, acquired focal oncogene amplifications and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletions were associated with an increase in chromosomal imbalances, which converged with markers of chromosomal instability such as chromothripsis and whole-genome doubling. In both types of IDH-mutant glioma, we observed a convergence of acquired alterations, genome-wide changes and worse patient outcomes, suggesting that treatment-refractory clones were being selected. Treatment with temozolomide was associated with the mutational signatures SBS11 and SBS119 in both tumour types, whereas the radiotherapy-associated ID8 signature increased in astrocytomas specifically. We show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumour progression and treatment in distinct ways, suggesting that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas differ in their responses to treatment-induced DNA damage.

items.title: Additional Analyses to Address Model Used to Adjust for Crossover in the ClarIDHy Trial
items.abstract: After publication of the Original Investigation, “Final Overall Survival Efficacy Results of Ivosidenib for Patients With Advanced Cholangiocarcinoma With IDH1 Mutation: The Phase 3 Randomized Clinical ClarIDHy Trial,” published online September 23, 2021, and in the November 2021 issue of JAMA Oncology, concern was raised about the rank-preserving structural failure time (RPSFT) model that was used to adjust for crossover. The analysis was redone with bootstrapping to calculate the 95% CIs for overall survival (OS). However, in this study, there were limited number of OS events after crossover in the placebo arm, which could impact the stability and precision of the bootstrapping for the CI calculation. Due to this issue, an additional ad hoc sensitivity analysis was performed to calculate CIs using RPSFT analysis without bootstrapping. When adjusted for crossover, based on bootstrapping, the median OS with placebo remained 5.1 months, but the corrected 95% CIs are 3.5 to 11.4 months. The hazard ratio remained 0.49, but the corrected 95% CIs are 0.25 to 1.24. Following the additional ad hoc sensitivity analysis without bootstrapping, the median OS was 5.1 months (95% CI, 3.8-7.6) with placebo (hazard ratio, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.34-0.70). Corrections have been made to the Abstract, Methods, Results, and Discussion sections; Figure 2; and the Visual Abstract. The authors have posted a Comment online to explain these corrections.

items.title: Blood-based biomarkers in patients with recurrent, persistent, or metastatic endometrial cancer treated with olaparib and cediranib: Results from NRG-GY012
items.authors: Nixon AB, Enserro DM, Bender DP, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The NRG‐GY012 phase 2 trial evaluated olaparib, cediranib, and the combination in 120 patients with recurrent, persistent, or metastatic endometrial cancer (EC). Predictive and prognostic associations between blood‐based biomarkers and clinical outcomes were assessed. Methods Plasma samples collected at baseline, cycle 4 day 1, and disease progression were analyzed for circulating protein biomarkers (Angiome). The primary analysis evaluated the predictive impact of IL‐6 on progression‐free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). The predictive and prognostic impact of all other markers on PFS and OS were also evaluated. Results Ninety‐six baseline plasma samples were included in this analysis. Results from GOG‐218 identified IL‐6 was predictive of clinical benefit using a threshold of 2.9 pg/mL. Although the 2.9 pg/mL cut point did not validate in GY012, IL‐6 associated with OS using the median level of 4.2 pg/mL as the cut point. Although patients with >4.2 pg/mL IL‐6 had worse prognosis, higher IL‐6 levels were associated with longer OS benefit in the cediranib arms (pintx = .085). In secondary analyses, osteopontin (OPN) and placental growth factor (PlGF) potentially predicted benefit. Patients with higher OPN levels had shorter OS in the olaparib arm, whereas patients with lower OPN had longer OS in the cediranib arms (pintx = .035). Patients with higher PlGF benefited more from cediranib (PFS, pintx = .030; OS, pintx = .024). Multiple prognostic markers were also identified. Conclusions IL‐6 may be predictive of outcome; OPN and PlGF represent novel potential predictive biomarkers, in EC patients receiving anti‐angiogenic therapy. Further evaluation is warranted.

items.title: Practical considerations in measuring out-of-field neutron dose for pulsed and gantry-mounted proton therapy machines
items.authors: Zhang H, Mazur TR, Zorloni G, et al.
items.abstract: Objective.Synchrocyclotrons deliver radiation in distinct macro pulses with high instantaneous dose rate that distinguish them from isochronous cyclotrons and synchrotrons. The relatively high instantaneous dose rates associated with synchrocyclotrons require special consideration in measurement of the neutron dose. The objective of this work is to measure the out-of-field neutron ambient dose equivalent (H*(10)) as a conservative operational surrogate to assess the fetal dose due to secondary neutrons for a gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron proton therapy system when an intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) brain treatment is delivered with the dynamic aperture (DA), static aperture (SA), and no aperture (NA).Approach.A pencil beam scanning (PBS) gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron was used for beam delivery. IMPT plans employing the DA, SA, and NA, each with 3 fields (vertex, lateral, and posterior-anterior (PA)) were optimized using the treatment planning system to treat a left-sided spherical brain target with 6 cm diameter to a total dose of 66 Gy (weighted by radiobiological effectiveness [RBE] 1.1) in 33 fractions. The plans were delivered to an anthropomorphic phantom and the neutron H*(10) was measured using two commercial rem-meters, a WENDI-II and a LUPIN-BF3-NP counter at 43, 53, 61, and 71 cm distance from the isocenter intended to mimic distances to a fetus at various gestational periods. To investigate the influence of the couch angle for the PA field, the neutron dose from the PA field was measured at several couch angles including 0°, 180°, and 270°.Main results.WENDI-II suffers from dead-time associated issues and underestimated the dose by a factor of ∼1.7-2.7 compared to LUPIN-BF3-NP. H*(10) showed dependence on the measurement location and the use of field shaping system. The total H*(10) for 66 Gy-equivalent proton dose was estimated to be 10.7 mSv (9.7 mSv) and 4.9 mSv (4.5 mSv) at 43 and 71 cm distance from the isocenter, respectively, when the SA (DA) was used. Without an aperture the corresponding values were 11.8 mSv and 5.3 mSv. The 270°-couch-angle resulted in the highest neutron dose from the PA field by ∼15% relative to the 0°-couch-angle, resulting in an increase in the neutron dose by ∼5% for the whole treatment.Significance.WENDI-II is not a reliable device for in-room neutron dose measurement for synchrocyclotrons with high instantaneous dose rates.…

items.title: Physics-informed machine learning-based dose calculation for patients undergoing fluoroscopically guided interventional procedures
items.authors: Han H, Griffin K, Saha M, et al.
items.abstract: To develop and evaluate a physics-informed machine-learning framework for rapid organ-dose estimation in fluoroscopically guided interventional procedures without requiring patient-specific imaging.Approach: We used 385 adult radiation dose structured reports from three procedure types-bilateral carotid angiography, percutaneous biliary drainage, and liver chemoembolization-comprising more than 50,000 irradiation events. A body-size-matched computational phantom was selected using patient sex, height, and weight. RDSR-derived beam parameters and engineered descriptors of beam-organ geometry and attenuation were used to train organ-specific XGBoost models for localized organs and a multi-output multilayer perceptron model for four distributed tissues. Monte Carlo-derived dose coefficients from NCIRF3 were used as target values.Main results: In the held-out test set of 12,683 irradiation events, 49.4% and 84.8% of XGBoost-based localized-organ estimates were within ±5% and ±20% of the Monte Carlo-derived values, respectively. The corresponding proportions were 88.2% and 98.0% for the distributed-tissue estimates and 87.6% and 98.3% for detriment-weighted dose. The median relative prediction error across organs and tissues was 0.37% (interquartile range, -3.68% to 4.99%). A reliability score was developed to support uncertainty-aware interpretation. The framework required approximately 0.3 s per irradiation event, corresponding to an approximately 290-fold acceleration relative to conventional Monte Carlo simulation under the benchmark conditions.Significance: The proposed image-free framework enables rapid organ-dose estimation when patient imaging is unavailable and may support large retrospective epidemiological studies and uncertainty-aware dose monitoring. Because development and validation were limited to three procedure types and relied on reconstructed phantom-beam geometry, external validation is required before application to other procedures or high-precision individual clinical decisions.

These drugs are already changing the standard of care in PDAC, and their development raises important questions about how ongoing and future trials of local therapies such as radiotherapy (RT) may be affected. Although RT remains part of the therapeutic armamentarium for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), particularly in locally advanced disease and the adjuvant setting, decades of clinical trials have raised more questions than they have answered.

items.title: Dosimetric Comparison of Five Radiotherapy Techniques in Left-Sided Breast Cancer Patients Following Breast-Conserving Surgery
items.authors: Zhang Y, Han A, Yang S, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: This study aims to compare and evaluate the dosimetric characteristics of five radiotherapy techniques in left-sided breast cancer patients following breast-conserving surgery. The five radiotherapy techniques include three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3D-CRT), fixed-field intensity-modulated radiation therapy (ff-IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), hybrid 3D-CRT with IMRT (CRT + IMRT), and hybrid 3D-CRT with VMAT (CRT + VMAT). Patients And Methods: Ten patients with left-sided breast cancer who received postlumpectomy radiotherapy at the Department of Radiation Oncology, First Hospital of Qinhuangdao, between June 1, 2020, and June 1, 2021, were randomly enrolled in this study. For each patient, five distinct treatment plans were designed using the five aforementioned techniques (3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, CRT + IMRT, and CRT + VMAT) based on identical computed tomography (CT) imaging datasets. Dosimetric parameters for the tumor target volume, organs at risk (OARs), and normal tissues (defined as body minus planning target volume [PTV], termed B-P) were analyzed and compared using dose-volume histograms (DVHs) and isodose distributions. Results: The CRT + VMAT technique demonstrated superior PTV dose coverage, conformity, and homogeneity compared to 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, and CRT + IMRT (p < 0.05). In contrast, the VMAT technique achieved significantly lower V30 (%) values for bilateral lungs and ipsilateral lung than 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, CRT + IMRT, and CRT + VMAT (p < 0.05). The CRT + IMRT technique reduced V5 (%) values for bilateral lungs, ipsilateral lung, and heart compared to 3D-CRT, ff-IMRT, VMAT, and CRT + VMAT (p < 0.05). Finally, 3D-CRT required the fewest monitor units (MUs) and shortest treatment time among all techniques (p < 0.05). Conclusion: Clinicians may tailor radiotherapy plans to individual patients based on the distinct dosimetric profiles of each technique. For patients requiring optimal PTV dose distribution, the CRT + VMAT technique is suggest. For enhanced cardiopulmonary protection (e.g., reduced lung/heart doses), ff-IMRT or CRT + IMRT may be prioritized. Additionally, 3D-CRT should be the first choice for patients needing rapid fractionated treatment due to its efficiency in minimizing MUs and treatment time.

items.title: Comparative Outcomes of Single- and Split-Fraction Low-Dose Radiation in Mycosis Fungoides
items.authors: Lange SJ, Trepanowski N, Ajmani A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Localized radiation is a cornerstone therapy for early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF), with low-dose regimens achieving high response rates. However, the optimal fractionation schedule remains unclear. Single-fraction (8 Gy × 1) and split-fraction (4 Gy × 2) regimens are widely used, but comparative data are limited. Reducing treatment burden may be particularly important in rural settings, where travel distance can limit access. Methods And Materials: This study aims to compare lesion-level response, recurrence, and durability between 8 Gy × 1 and 4 Gy × 2 low-dose radiation regimens in MF. We performed a retrospective review of 136 lesions from 27 adults with biopsy-confirmed MF treated with localized electron beam radiation at a rural multidisciplinary cutaneous lymphoma clinic (2014-2025). Lesions were categorized as patch or plaque. The primary outcome was complete response (CR) at 6 months. Secondary outcomes included overall response rate, local recurrence, time to next therapy, and toxicity. Analyses included χ²/Fisher's exact tests, Kaplan-Meier survival, Cox regression, and inverse-probability weighting. Results: Of 136 lesions, 119 (87.5%) received 4 Gy × 2 and 17 (12.5%) received 8 Gy × 1. Six-month CR was 81.5% versus 82.4%, respectively (P = 1.0). Overall response rate was 98.3% versus 100%, respectively (P = 1.0). Six-month local recurrence occurred in 3.4% versus 11.8% of lesions (P = .17), and additional local treatment within 6 months was required in 12.6% versus 5.9% of lesions (P = .69). No grade ≥2 toxicities occurred. Median patient travel distance was 86.2 miles versus 71.0 miles (P = .069). Multivariable and inverse-probability weighting analyses showed no association between regimen and CR at 6 months. Conclusions: Limitations of this study include retrospective design and small single-fraction sample. Single-fraction 8 Gy was associated with similar short-term outcomes and excellent tolerability, supporting its use as an effective, logistically advantageous option, particularly in rural practice.

items.title: 8th International consensus guidelines for the management of advanced breast cancer (ABC8 guidelines)
items.authors: Cardoso F, Ribeiro JM, Schumacher-Wulf E, et al.
items.abstract: The Advanced Breast Cancer (ABC) 8th international consensus conference took place on 6-8 November 2025, in Lisbon, and updated the previous ABC international consensus guidelines that are described in this manuscript. These guidelines reflect the work of a large and global consensus panel, comprising healthcare professionals and patients, and provide recommendations on how to best manage patients with advanced breast cancer (inoperable locally advanced or metastatic), of all breast cancer subtypes. The guidelines are based on the best available evidence or on expert opinion when a higher level of evidence is lacking and aim to cover the needs of the person living with ABC, including but also beyond the main therapeutic recommendations. Each guideline is accompanied by the level of evidence (LoE), the grade of recommendation (GoR), and the percentage of consensus reached at the consensus session. Updated diagnostic and treatment algorithms are also provided. These guidelines are endorsed by several international oncology organizations (AGO, AORTIC, ECO, EONS, ESO, ESTRO, EUSOMA, GECO Perú, SUMA, MASCC, French Breast Cancer Guidelines and AMAAC) and have official representation from ASCO, NCCN and ABC-NZ. Inequalities in access to high-quality care have increased in the last decade, both between and within countries, and are a major concern. The ABC guidelines provide guidance on the best available management options for patients living with ABC globally, assuming availability of the recommended therapies. Their adaptation is often needed in resource-constrained settings, and the grading of each recommendation may help in prioritizing access to available options.

items.title: Integration of an echocardiographic motion-management system into photon-based stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation planning
items.authors: Oppitz H, Matusche AL, Mantovani L, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Cardiorespiratory ultrasound motion monitoring may enhance the precision of dose delivery for stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation (STAR) of ventricular tachycardia. This treatment planning study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of photon-based STAR planning in the presence of an ultrasound probe. Materials And Methods: For sixteen targets in fourteen patients, three treatment plans were retrospectively created and compared: a reference plan without an ultrasound probe and two plans in which the ultrasound probe was spared from the primary treatment beam (apical or parasternal probe positions). Descriptive and statistical analyses were performed for target/organ dose-volume and treatment beam metrics, conformity-indices and maximum probe exposure. Results: The ultrasound probe could be spared from the primary beam in all cases with D0.035 cm³ < 1 Gy (median 0.2 Gy with apical and 0.4 Gy with parasternal placement) with slightly elevated organ dose-volume metrics and no significant differences in target dose-volume metrics. The conformity-index (50 % isodose line) differed significantly for apical and parasternal probe position (median reference plan 4.0 vs. 5.0 and 4.5, respectively; p < 0.01). The parasternal position gave slightly superior results compared to the apical position (e.g., heart minus planning target volume V12.5 Gy 7.6 % [4.7-13.3] vs. 8.2 % [6.4-12.5]; left lung V10 Gy 3.4 % [1.0-4.5] vs. 4.2 % [1.6-6.8]), albeit in all plans dose guidance parameters remained within clinically acceptable limits. Conclusions: The ultrasound probe could be spared from the primary beam without compromising photon-based STAR plan quality beyond clinically acceptable deviations. The results support further investigation of ultrasound-based STAR motion management.

items.title: Convolutional neural network metal artifact reduction in ultra-high resolution photon counting detector CT of middle- and inner-ear implants
items.authors: Treb KJ, Sadeghian M, Cao W, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Metallic inner‐ and middle‐ear implants with submillimeter structures requiring ultra‐high resolution (UHR) imaging invariably result in metal artifacts at CT, which can obscure adjacent microstructures and subtle pathologic findings. Current metal artifact reduction techniques can be less effective for small metal objects or metal in heterogeneous background anatomy, and can sometimes introduce new artifacts or noise. Purpose To develop and evaluate an image‐domain convolutional neural network to reduce metal artifacts near inner‐ and middle‐ear implants in UHR photon‐counting‐detector (PCD)‐CT. Methods For network training, three stapes prosthesis models containing titanium and platinum were randomly oriented within a head‐sized phantom and imaged on a PCD‐CT with a UHR protocol. Metal and metal+artifact images were isolated by subtraction of the phantom background followed by CT number thresholding. Isolated artifact signal was enhanced via multiplication with a randomized factor ranging from one to a pre‐determined artifact amplification scalar hyperparameter. Paired training inputs (with artifacts) and labels (without artifacts) were created by adding metal‐free patient temporal bone images with metal+artifact and metal images, respectively. Combinations of 9 patient CT volumes and 24 metal CT volumes were used to create 216 CT volumes for training and validation with an 80%/20% training/validation split. The network was retrained with different amplification scalars (5, 10, 20, 30, 40) and with either mean‐squared‐error or mean‐absolute‐error loss functions to determine the optimal combination of these hyperparameters. The network was tested on 7 CT volumes from patients with three different implant types: stapes prostheses, cochlear implants, and a transverse sinus stent. Network performance was quantified through the artifact index, noise magnitude, CT number preservation of metal and bone, and dimensions of metal measured as the full‐width at half‐maximum of CT number line profiles. Results Networks trained with mean‐squared‐error demonstrated a trade‐off between metal artifact reduction and preservation of bone CT number as the artifact amplification scalar changed. The trade‐off was not observed when mean‐absolute error was used. Using the network with hyperparameters that best preserved bone and reduced artifacts simultaneously (mean‐absolute‐error, amplification scalar 20), the artifact index was improved by 83.2% (p < 0.001) across all implant types, and image noise was reduced by 46.8% (p < 0.001).…

items.title: Longitudinal trends in Gamma Knife radiosurgery utilization across multiple technological generations: A Single-Institution Observational Study
items.authors: El Basha D, Filiput E, Curcuru A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) has been a foundational modality for the treatment of intracranial diseases for several decades, with successive platform generations introducing substantial technological advancements. Improvements in source configuration, patient positioning systems, imaging guidance, and immobilization techniques have expanded clinical capabilities. Despite these ongoing innovations, few long-term institutional analyses have evaluated whether GKRS utilization has remained stable, increased, or shifted with changes in disease patterns and retreatment needs over time. Purpose: Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) has undergone multiple technological evolutions over the past two decades. This study provides a retrospective analysis of longitudinal utilization at a single institution, examining trends in case volume, disease indications, retreatment frequency, and platform era. Methods: A retrospective analysis of Gamma Knife treatments delivered at one institution between 1998 and 2025 was performed. Annual counts of first, repeat, and total GKRS treatments were analyzed using negative binomial regression with a log link and Newey-West standard errors; platform-adjusted models accounted for the sequential relationship between calendar time and platform era. Segmented negative binomial regression of monthly counts evaluated slope changes at platform transitions. Results: Across the study period, 6,201 unique patients received 7,267 delivered treatment courses. Median annual treatment volume was 276 procedures (range, 71-362); median age at first treatment was 60 years (IQR, 50-69), and brain metastasis was the primary indication in 2,991 patients (48.2%). Total volume increased in unadjusted modeling (count ratio [CR], 1.03; p < 0.001), and repeat treatments showed the strongest platform-adjusted growth (CR 1.14; p < 0.001). Metastatic disease was the dominant adjusted disease-specific trend (CR 1.08; p = 0.01). Repeat metastatic treatments increased more than overall repeat treatments (CR 1.15; p < 0.001). Segmented regression showed significant growth during the baseline Model B era (annualized CR 1.16; p < 0.001) followed by significant attenuation at the Model C transition (annualized CR 0.90; p = 0.01). The primary segmented model showed no significant incremental slope change at Perfexion or Icon; sensitivity analyses indicated that the estimated Icon-era association was model-dependent.…

items.title: Automated linac downtime tracking across 4 radiation oncology clinics within a single hospital system utilizing statistical process control
items.authors: Serafini CE, Thomas M, Yang X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Linear accelerator (linac) downtime disrupts clinical workflow and may delay patient treatment; however, downtime events are frequently undocumented or recorded in informal reporting systems. Data-driven approaches using routinely collected operational metrics may improve downtime surveillance and provide insight into system-level adaptation. Purpose: This study aims to evaluate if statistical process control (SPC) methods can be applied to routine treatment and scheduling data from an oncology information system (OIS) to identify linac downtime events and characterize operational response across multiple radiation oncology clinics within a single hospital system. Methods: Daily machine-level operational data from 10 linacs across 4 clinics were analyzed over 29 months (January 2024-May 2026). Machine metrics included daily patient volume, cancellations, and operating hours. For each machine, rolling 45-day baseline means and standard deviations were computed, and SPC rules (± 3σ control limits and > 10 cancellations / day) were applied to detect downtime days. SPC-flagged events were compared with email-based downtime event logs to calculate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Downtime events were categorized by cause, and intra-hospital patient redistribution was assessed by identifying concurrent > 4σ volume increases on alternate machines. Results: Over the 29-month study period, 138 downtime events were documented in downtime event logs. SPC identified 23 additional events exhibiting operational signatures consistent with downtime. Using reported events as the reference standard, SPC achieved sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.99, PPV 0.79, and NPV 0.99. Downtime frequently resulted in compensatory increases in patient volume on alternate machines, with 41 transfer pairs identified across three hospitals. When the reported downtime cause was specified, machine mechanical causes accounted for the largest proportion (48%) of downtime events. Conclusions: SPC applied to routinely collected operational data provides a scalable framework for automated linac downtime detection. Integration of automated monitoring with structured reporting may improve downtime surveillance and inform proactive operational planning in radiation oncology.

items.title: Machine learning predictors of post-radiotherapy cardiotoxicity in a Latin American breast cancer cohort: Clinical risk factors outperform cardiac dosimetry
items.authors: Aguirre-Bravo V, El Far R, Herrera Ruiz M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Most evidence on post-radiotherapy cardiotoxicity (CDT) derives from Global North cohorts, and the relative contribution of baseline clinical risk versus cardiac dosimetry remains poorly characterized in Latin American populations. Purpose: To examine, in a Chilean breast cancer cohort, whether baseline clinical risk factors or cardiac dose-volume metrics better predict post-RT cardiac events, using supervised and unsupervised learning. Methods: Retrospective cohort of 42 breast cancer patients treated with thoracic radiotherapy (RT, median heart dose 2.6 Gy; median follow-up 84.4 months). CDT was defined per CTCAE v5.0 ( ≥ Grade 1), excluding Grade 1 events coded under the non-specific term "Cardiac disorders - Other, specify", which on review were incidental imaging findings. Dose-volume histogram (DVH) parameters from seven cardiac substructures were extracted. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for prediction, principal component analysis (PCA) and kernel PCA for exploratory clustering, and bootstrap 0.632+ for optimism correction. The 2023 American Heart Association (AHA) PREVENT score was evaluated post hoc. Results: Ten patients (23.8%) developed CDT and 16 (38.1%) experienced cardiovascular events. No DVH differences were found between CDT+ and CDT- groups across any cardiac structure (all p > 0.05  ), although the design is powered only for large effects. By contrast, IMRT delivered significantly higher cardiac doses than 3D-CRT across multiple substructures, without a differential CDT rate. Pre-existing cardiovascular disease was the strongest predictor (crude OR = 6.50, p = 0.020  ; adjusted OR = 2.08, 95% CI 1.03-4.16, p = 0.040  ). The median time to the first CTCAE-graded event was 48.4 months. The clinical-only model reached an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.783 versus 0.604 for dosimetry alone; the combined model corrected to 0.649 (95% CI 0.204-0.933). The AHA PREVENT score showed no significant risk gradient (trend p = 0.203  ) but was markedly less susceptible to overfitting than DVH-only models (optimism 0.089 vs. 0.194). Conclusions: In this low-cardiac-dose cohort, baseline clinical variables outperformed cardiac dose-volume metrics in predicting post-RT cardiac events, although the design was not powered to exclude a dose-effect relationship at these exposures. Registry-based baseline risk assessment is therefore the more robust starting point in this setting, and IMRT breast RT planning warrants multi-substructure cardiac dosimetry monitoring.

items.title: Supplemental Breast Cancer Screening with Contrast-enhanced Mammography or Abbreviated MRI for Extremely Dense Breasts: The DENSE-2 Trial
items.authors: van Grinsven SEL, Monninkhof EM, Mann RM, et al.
items.abstract: Women with extremely dense breasts have an increased risk of breast cancer but also a decreased sensitivity of mammography. The Dense Tissue and Early Breast Neoplasm Screening (DENSE) trial, initiated in 2011, showed that supplemental full-protocol MRI screening reduced the number of interval cancers in women with extremely dense breasts. Cost-effective screening scenarios have been described, but imaging costs and capacity remain barriers to implementing full-protocol MRI in population-based breast cancer screening programs. Therefore, the DENSE-2 trial was set up to investigate two alternate screening techniques, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) or abbreviated MRI (AB-MRI), that are expected to be cheaper and to make more efficient use of the available capacity while potentially achieving similar results to full-protocol MRI. DENSE-2 is a multicenter randomized controlled trial embedded in the Dutch screening program. It comprises two consecutive screening rounds in which women receive the same breast imaging technique both times. The trial investigates the value of supplemental screening with CEM or AB-MRI in women with extremely dense breasts with a negative screening mammogram. The primary aim is to determine whether these methods will lead to a reduction of interval cancers compared with mammography. The DENSE-2 trial results will provide insights into the performance, feasibility, and acceptability of both screening modalities, enable long-term outcome modeling, and support decision-making on the most appropriate screening strategy for women with extremely dense breasts. items.title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Clinical and Genomic Prognostic Factors for Progression-Free Survival in Metastatic Breast Cancer Using Phase III MONALEESA Trials
items.authors: Wang, C., Paul, R., Li, Y., Smith, S., Cao, Q., Chang, S. H., Charlab, R., Coroller, T., Huang, R., Amiri-Kordestani, L., Li, Z., Liu, Q., Osgood, C., Peyrard, S., Sahiner, B., Santana-Quintero, L., Su, F., Zarate, J. P., Zhu, H., Ohlssen, D., Petrick, N., Amatya, A., Solovieff, N.
items.abstract: PurposeCyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors in combination with endocrine therapy have become widely adopted as a first-line treatment approach for hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) advanced breast cancer (ABC). Through a collaboration between Novartis and the US Food and Drug Administration, we integrated multimodal data from phase III MONALEESA trials to identify novel prognostic factors for HR+/HER2-ABC. Experimental DesignBaseline clinical and genomics data were collected from patients in the MONALEESA-2, -3, and -7 trials. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma samples and gene expression in archival tumor biopsies were analyzed. Machine learning models were trained (n = 1,355) on progression-free survival (PFS) using multimodal features via fusion models. In a test set (n = 382), prognostic performances were evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier, Cox, and Weibull models. ResultsThe late fusion model achieved a prognostic performance (C-index: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.641-0.799) slightly outperforming early fusion (C-index: 0.718, 95% CI: 0.631-0.791) and single-modality models. Model-based risk stratification identified distinct low- and high-risk groups (PFS HR, 0.28; 95% CI: 0.20-0.38). Among the top 40 features for progression risk (18 clinical, 20 gene expression, and 2 ctDNA), these were associated with higher risk: liver involvement, higher histological grades, early relapse; lower STC2 and RBBP8 expressions and higher FBX05 expression; and higher tumor mutational burden and ctDNA purity. ConclusionsIntegrating clinical and genomic modalities improved progression risk prediction compared with single-modality models, while highlighting salient features that inform the underlying biology and support hypothesis generation.

items.title: Germline DDX41 defines a distinct subgroup in MDS undergoing transplantation with reduced relapse and improved survival
items.authors: Gagelmann N, Reilly CR, Sasi A, et al.
items.abstract: Germline DDX41 variants are a recognized cause of adult myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS), characterized by distinct biological features and favorable prognosis. The independent effect of DDX41 status on outcomes after allogeneic transplantation, the role of conditioning intensity, and treatment-related toxicity risk remain unresolved. To address this gap, we analyzed 1,514 patients with MDS undergoing transplantation prior to routine DDX41 testing alongside a wild-type comparator, providing an unbiased benchmark for this molecular subgroup. Forty-nine patients (3.2%) carried pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) germline DDX41 variants; 19 (39%) had an additional somatic DDX41 mutation, most commonly p.R525H. P/LP DDX41 cases were older (median 63 vs 59 years) and showed lower IPSS-M risk with absent TP53 mutations (0% vs 21%). In terms of outcome, 2-year relapse incidence was significantly lower in P/LP DDX41 (17% vs 34%, p=0.01). In multivariable analysis, the presence of a DDX41 P/LP variant independently associated with lower risk of relapse (hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.88; p=0.02), concentrated in the reduced-intensity/nonmyeloablative stratum. Adjusted models showed significantly improved disease-free survival (DFS) for P/LP DDX41 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95; p=0.03) and no significant association with non-relapse mortality (NRM) or graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). In summary, these findings identify DDX41-associated MDS as a transplant subgroup with superior DFS regardless of conditioning intensity driven by reduced relapse risk and lack of excess NRM and GVHD supporting incorporation of germline DDX41 status into transplant planning.

items.title: Cancer risks associated with BRCA1 and BRCA2: Overview and management
items.authors:
Kelsey E. Breen, 
Shagun Vashisth, 
Ying L. Liu
items.abstract: Abstract The BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes are integral to the repair of DNA double‐strand breaks. Therefore, germline pathogenic variants (PVs) in either of these genes are associated with an increased risk of developing hereditary cancers. For over 30 years, studies have demonstrated a well established and markedly increased lifetime risk of female breast cancer and ovarian cancer for individuals with a PV in BRCA1 or BRCA2. Additional canonical cancers include prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer for males and females, and male breast cancer. Several noncanonical cancers have also been reported in association with BRCA1 or BRCA2, including stomach cancer and endometrial cancer. This review summarizes the established and evolving cancer risks associated with germline PVs in BRCA1 or BRCA2 as well as current clinical management recommendations. With increased uptake and diversified utility of germline genetic testing, this summary provides a current overview for clinical management of both male and female individuals with a PV in BRCA1 or BRCA2.

items.title: Selective lipid metabolic remodelling in radiosensitive normal tissues after FLASH radiotherapy
items.authors: Aramaki S, Dubail M, Sertorio M, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: FLASH radiotherapy, delivered at ultra-high dose rates, spares normal tissues while maintaining tumor control, but the molecular basis of this differential response remains poorly defined, particularly at timepoints relevant to tissue repair. We investigated whether lipid metabolism contributes to the FLASH effect in head and neck cancer. Materials And Methods: MOC2 tumor-bearing mice received a single 10 Gy fraction of conventional (CONV) or ultra-high dose-rate FLASH protons, with non-irradiated controls (CTRL). Tongue and contralateral tumors were collected two weeks later and analyzed by bulk lipidomics, spatial lipidomics and proteomics. After biochemical filtering, 1,547 lipid species across 37 classes were quantified. Results: At two weeks, CONV irradiation was associated with a triglyceride-catabolic, oxidative-stress signature in tongue tissue, marked by loss of the lipid-droplet hydrolase Ces1d alongside induction of the peroxisomal β-oxidation enzyme Acox1. FLASH irradiation was instead associated with a distinct lipid-remodelling signature: suppression of Mgll, induction of Apoe, membrane phospholipid remodelling (increased phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine), and Lypla2 upregulation. Spatial lipidomics provided illustrative spatial context consistent with concentration of these changes in minor salivary gland acini. Tumor tissue showed no comparable modality-specific divergence. Conclusions: These correlative multi-omics data indicate that FLASH is associated with remodelling of lipid metabolism in radiosensitive normal tissue, beyond a simple reduction of acute oxidative damage. We propose a Lipid Metabolic Remodelling Hypothesis for testing: the remodelling of lipid metabolism observed after FLASH may contribute to normal-tissue sparing rather than representing solely a downstream consequence of reduced acute oxidative damage. This model complements existing physicochemical models and offers a basis for radioprotection strategies in head and neck radiotherapy.

items.title: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in ovarian cancer: a phase 1 trial
items.authors: Sellars MC, Frank JA, Shim B, et al.
items.abstract: Personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines in the adjuvant setting are of increasing interest across malignancies. Here we report the results of a phase 1 clinical trial testing the feasibility and safety of personalized neoantigen-targeting cancer vaccines for high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer. 'NeoVax' consisted of pools of synthetic long peptides targeting patient-specific neoantigens admixed with the immunostimulant poly-ICLC, was combined with delayed administration of anti-PD-1 antibody, and was tested in ten patients (one newly diagnosed patient (Cohort A) and nine patients at first recurrence (Cohort B)) with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer following standard-of-care platinum doublet chemotherapy. Nine of 12 evaluable Cohort B patients were vaccinated (75%, 90% CI 47-93%) and 1 of 9 Cohort A patients (11%, 90% CI 0.6-43%). No unexpected safety signals were encountered and no patients discontinued treatment due to toxicity. Across patients, >70% selected targets remained detectable by noninvasive cell-free DNA analysis despite a median of 6.5 months from the time of diagnostic biopsy to vaccine administration, during which, patients received standard-of-care chemotherapy. Biomarker analysis was suggestive of biologic activity of the vaccine in six of ten patients and this was associated with broader tumor and vaccine-specific immune responses in blood and tumor following vaccination. Resistant tumor clones reflected diverse mechanisms affecting antigen presentation, indicative of immune-selective pressure exerted by vaccination. Overall, the interplay between the repertoire of antigens presented by the tumor and the breadth of induced immunity seemed to dictate clinical efficacy following vaccination. items.title: Cancer Care Navigation Improves Timeliness of Treatment in Head and Neck Cancer
items.authors: Islam AM, Baldwin RB, Dallas AE, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Timely access to oncologic care is critical for patients with head and neck cancer (HNC), yet delays in treatment remain widespread. We sought to determine whether implementation of a care navigation program was associated with improved timeliness. Methods Four hunded and four adult patients who underwent HNC resection with free flap reconstruction were retrospectively reviewed. The primary outcome was time to adjuvant therapy and disease‐free survival. Results Median [IQR] age was 64 [58–73] years and 133 (33%) were women. Significant interval decreases were observed from surgery to initiation of adjuvant radiotherapy (56 [39–83] vs. 45 [31–64] days, p = 0.004). Log‐rank testing revealed no difference in disease‐free survival between pre‐ and postprogram cohorts (p = 0.7695). Conclusions Implementation of a care navigation program was associated with significant reductions in time to treatment. These findings suggest that structured pathways can meaningfully improve oncologic care delivery for HNC patients.

items.authors: Gustavo A. Viani, Ana Carolina Hamamura, Caio Viani Arruda, Carlos E. Cardoso, Helio A. Salmon, Gustavo O. Amaral
items.abstract: Post-mastectomy radiotherapy reduces locoregional recurrence and, where baseline risk is sufficient, improves breast cancer survival. Guidelines recommend it for women with four or more involved axillary nodes or locally advanced tumours[1]. Recurrence risk, however, is graded rather than dichotomous: pooled trial data show an absolute 15-year breast cancer mortality reduction of about 4-5% in women with four or more positive nodes but only 2-3% in those with one to three[2], reflecting the additional influence of tumour size, grade, and lymphovascular invasion.

items.authors: Honghan Wu, Zhi Wang
items.abstract: Intrapartum hypoxic injury remains one of the most consequential complications in modern obstetric care. It is a leading cause of stillbirth, neonatal death, and lifelong disability, and, in the UK, accounts for litigation costs that exceed the cost of maternity care itself.1 Cardiotocography has been the principal tool for detecting fetal compromise during labour for the past half century, yet it offers little clinical utility; admission cardiotocography screening alone has shown low sensitivity and high false-positive rates for the rare but catastrophic outcomes that matter most, such as hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, intrapartum stillbirth, and neonatal death.

items.title: Flow MRD pre-blinatumomab consolidation, despite subsequent clearance, is associated with inferior survival in Ph+ B-ALL
items.authors: Frost BF, Valtis YK, Flamand Y, et al.
items.abstract: Although adults with Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) may achieve a measurable residual disease-negative (MRD-) complete response (CR) after frontline treatment and blinatumomab (blina) consolidation, survival outcomes are heterogeneous, and known prognostic factors are limited. We conducted a retrospective, multicenter study of 81 adults with Ph+ B-ALL in MRD- (<10-4) CR1 after blina consolidation and stratified them by pre-blina MRD status as determined by multiparametric flow cytometry (flow). Patients who were pre-blina flow MRD- (n = 56) and flow MRD+ (n = 25) had similar baseline characteristics. With a median follow-up of 31.0 months, pre-blina flow MRD- patients had superior disease-free (DFS) and overall survival (OS) on univariate (p = 0.049 and p = 0.045, respectively) and multivariable analyses (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.08-0.87 and HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.03-0.90, respectively) relative to pre-blina flow MRD+ patients. Inferior DFS was seen with the IKZF1-plus genotype (HR 3.51, 95% CI 1.08-11.44) and extramedullary disease at diagnosis (HR 3.90, 95% CI 1.19-12.73). In exploratory analyses, pre-blina flow MRD+ status remained associated with inferior DFS (p = 0.0005) and OS (p < 0.0001) for patients who did not receive a subsequent hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) in CR1, but not in patients who did (p = 0.55 and p = 0.99, respectively). In summary, flow MRD+ status before blina consolidation was associated with inferior survival in patients with Ph+ B-ALL in CR1 despite subsequent clearance, and consolidative HCT may reduce this prognostic effect.

items.title: Optimization of catheter placement for interstitial gynecological brachytherapy with centroidal Voronoi tessellation
items.authors: Bennett J, Bélanger C, Chatigny PY, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the feasibility of using images taken after placement of the Template and APPlicator (post-TAPP) with a geometry-based catheter placement optimization to generate interstitial implants in locally advanced cervical cancer cases. Methods And Materials: A processing pipeline with Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT)-based catheter optimization was used to retrospectively simulate optimized catheters on post-TAPP imaging from 32 cervix transperinneal interstitial brachytherapy cases using a Syed Neblett template (16 with iterative MR-guidance, 16 without). Treatment plans were generated with CVT-optimized and clinically implanted catheters. Improvement in plan quality and decrease in number of inserted catheters due to catheter optimization were evaluated against cases performed with and without intraoperative MR imaging. Results: Use of CVT resulted in fewer unused catheters (mean reduction of ∼3) compared to the clinical cases performed both with and without MR imaging guidance, without an increase in %V150 or %V200. In non-MR-guided cases, use of CVT improved the EMBRACE-II limit compliance for D90% for CTVHR. This improvement was not observed in MR-guided procedures. Conclusion: This feasibility study suggests that post-TAPP CVT catheter optimization can achieve clinically acceptable dosimetry while limiting unnecessary catheters, showing a qualitative improvement in dosimetry compared to using preBrachy images alone for catheter selection.
